Ablation study validates the effectiveness of bidirectional structure: introducing bidirectional structure improves all metrics for both tasks (see 1st and 3rd rows of Table 3). 7.Clarification of region-specific inputs (R2Q2) Our region-specific inputs are generated from the whole tongue image with a simple rule-based partition: using image center as reference and partition the tongue into upper/lower, left/right strip regions and a central region as organ-related cropped regions. This requires no extra supervision, segmentation model, or manual annotation. 8.External validation(R4Q5) TongueDx is the only public dataset supporting both syndrome and organ tasks. Note that it includes images from multiple devices and diverse age groups, providing certain diversity. Future work involves multi-center validation to evaluate generalization. 9.Imbalance(R1Q3) We use the inverse positive sample ratio as class weight in weighted BCE loss.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend rebuttal rather than early accept, deviating from R1 (5/Accept) and R2 (4/Weak Accept) and aligning more closely with R4 (3/Weak Reject). The deviation is justified by a paper-grounded concern that R1 and R2 did not test, but which would materially overturn the headline empirical claim if confirmed. Per MICCAI guidelines, mixed scores (5, 4, 3) do not satisfy the “all ≥4” rule for early accept, and one of the negative concerns is decisive enough to require a rebuttal cycle for the following reasons. 1.Subject-disjoint splitting is not stated and is almost certainly violated. The paper reports a 3,371/843/895 sample-level train/val/test split (Sec. 3.1) on the TongueDx dataset, which the authors describe as 5,109 images from 465 subjects — i.e., ~11 images per subject on average. Sec. 3.1 is silent on whether the split is subject-disjoint. Under any random sample-level split with this image-to-subject ratio, the same patient almost certainly appears in train, val, and test. If true, all reported numbers are inflated. This is the central concern raised by R4, and reading the paper directly confirms it as a verifiable gap rather than a subjective worry. 2.The reported gains are modest enough to disappear under correct splitting. The proposed method beats the second-best baseline by only +1.60 F1 on syndrome and +0.47 F1 on organ tasks (Table 1) — well within the range that subject leakage could account for. Until the splitting protocol is clarified, the empirical contribution is unverifiable. | Two reviewers support acceptance based on the novelty and clinical relevance of the joint modeling design, while R4 raises concerns about data-protocol transparency. I agree with the majority view that the methodological contribution justifies acceptance, but the following should be clarified in the camera-ready: (i) confirm whether the 3,371/843/895 train/val/test split on TongueDx (5,109 images / 465 subjects, Sec. 3.1) is subject-disjoint, and if not, re-run under subject-disjoint splitting; (ii) document the MLLM (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct) usage, including prompts, freezing strategy, language, input format, and how H_MLLM is injected, with an ablation isolating the MLLM contribution from the adapter capacity; (iii) provide annotation provenance for the five organ-abnormality labels, describe how syndrome-local and organ-local image branches are constructed, and report statistical significance tests on the gains given the small subject pool. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes an MLLM-enhanced region-aware bidirectional evidence-based model for tongue diagnosis. Different from prior work that models syndrome patterns and organ status in isolation, the study jointly learns their intrinsic correlation through unified representation learning and joint inference. The topic is clinically important and the bidirectional evidence-based design is well motivated. During the rebuttal phase, the authors satisfactorily clarified the critical subject-disjoint splitting protocol, resolving a central concern that threatened the validity of the main results. Reviewer #4 and Reviewer #1 now explicitly recommend acceptance, and Reviewer #2 raises only limited, addressable concerns regarding the explanation of how partitioned regions are associated with organ-level features. Given that the major experimental validity issue has been resolved and the majority of reviewers support acceptance, I recommend accept. For the camera-ready version, the authors must: (1) reinstate confidence intervals and statistical tests; (2) substantially improve the clarity of the methodology, especially the association between region-based partitioning and organ-level feature semantics; (3) add or properly discuss appropriate multimodal or multi-region baselines; and (4) ensure that all standard experimental details and data splitting procedures are explicitly reported. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal resolved the main concerns sufficiently. In particular, the authors clarified the subject-level split, correcting what was previously the most serious issue, and explained the provenance of the organ labels as expert TCM annotations. They also provided a concrete description of how the MLLM is used in the pipeline and clarified that the region-specific inputs are obtained via a simple rule-based partition rather than requiring additional supervision or segmentation models. Some concerns remain, especially regarding moderate novelty, limited external validation, and the clinical meaning of the rule-based organ partitions. However, these do not outweigh the paper’s strengths.

title: Multi-Disease Diagnosis in Retinal Images via Patch-Level Reasoning and Selective Aggregation
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem. In real clinical settings, multiple retinal diseases often co-occur, and the discussion of lesion–disease mismatching is well motivated. (2) The proposed method is conceptually clear and easy to follow. The combination of disease-specific patch-level reasoning with selective aggregation is intuitive and well aligned with the problem setting. (3) The experimental results are generally solid. The proposed method shows consistent improvements over strong baselines across two datasets with different imaging modalities. In particular, the conditional evaluation in Section 3.4 is well designed, as it directly supports the central claim of reducing spurious associations under disease co-occurrence.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The method appears to be somewhat sensitive to the choice of Top-K, and the selection strategy could be further clarified and better justified. (2) While the evidence for improved interpretability and robustness to lesion–disease mismatching is encouraging, it remains somewhat preliminary. Providing quantitative evidence that the selected patches correspond to clinically meaningful disease regions would make this claim more convincing.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Well-motivated problem 2.Sound experimental design 3.Consistent improvements across two modalities 4.Interpretability via patch-level attribution
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty. The pipeline (CNN patch encoder → transformer decoder with disease-specific queries → patch-level prediction → top-K MIL aggregation) assembles well-established components. Patch-level prediction with MIL aggregation is a mature paradigm in computational pathology (e.g., CLAM [Lu et al., 2021], DSMIL [Li et al., CVPR 2021], TransMIL [Shao et al., NeurIPS 2021]). The disease-specific query mechanism closely resembles Q2L [14], which the authors acknowledge; the primary difference is replacing global pooling with top-K selection. This substitution, while reasonable, constitutes incremental modification rather than a conceptual advance. 2.Marginal quantitative improvements without statistical validation. The reported mAUC gains are +0.84% on LID-FFA and +1.01% on ODIR-5K. Improvements of this magnitude can fall within random variance across training runs. No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests are reported. Without such validation, it is unclear whether the improvements are reliable or merely stochastic. 3.Only two datasets are used, both from the retinal imaging domain. No experiments on other multi-label medical imaging benchmarks (e.g., chest X-ray with CheXpert/MIMIC-CXR, or dermatology) are provided to support the claimed generalizability. Additionally, all experiments use a single backbone (DenseNet121), which is not a commonly-evaluated backbone. It would be useful to clarify the selection reason, such as following the previous works or benchmarks. Testing on diverse architectures (e.g., ResNet, ViT) would strengthen the generalization claim. 4.The “first unified framework” claim is not well-supported. The paper states “To our knowledge, MD-PRSA is the first unified framework that combines disease localization with disease-specific feature modeling for multi-disease retinal diagnosis.” However, prior works such as CABNet [7] (cited by the authors) and attention-guided methods already combine spatial localization with disease-specific classification. This claim needs more careful qualification or stronger evidence of distinction. 5.Insufficient analysis of the top-K hyperparameter. The top-K selection is central to the MIL aggregation, yet K=10 for LID-FFA and K=50 for ODIR-5K are used with limited justification. The ablation (Table 2) shows sensitivity to K, but does not explain why optimal K differs by 5× across datasets or how to select K for a new dataset without exhaustive search. A principled or adaptive selection mechanism would strengthen the approach. Others: The introduction contains a typo (“In summury”)
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper identifies and explicitly defines a critical pathology in multi-disease diagnosis: “co-occurrence-induced lesion-disease mismatching.” 2.The method achieves State-of-the-Art (SOTA) results on two challenging datasets with different modalities.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The comparison methods are mostly common methods in multi-label domains, lacking specialized methods for the field of retinal diseases. 2.The performance of the model is highly dependent on the choice of K (the number of top patches selected). While the authors discuss this in the ablation study, the optimal K differs significantly between datasets (K=10 vs K=50). 3.For high-resolution retinal images, the Transformer decoder with cross-attention could lead to significant computational overhead compared to simpler CNN baselines. Its computational complexity shoud be discussed.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and positive recognition of the clinical importance of co-occurrence-induced lesion–disease mismatching, the interpretability of the proposed framework, and the overall experimental design. We address the main concerns below. 1.Clarification of the novelty (R2) The novelty of this work lies not in introducing entirely new architectural components, but in formulating and addressing a previously under-discussed problem in multi-disease retinal diagnosis: co-occurrence-induced lesion–disease mismatching, directly evaluated through the conditional evaluation protocol in Sec.3.4 and Fig.3.Existing MIL-based methods (e.g., CLAM, DSMIL, TransMIL) are primarily designed for binary or multi-class bag classification, where identifying discriminative instances is sufficient for bag-level prediction. In contrast, multi-label retinal diagnosis involves multiple co-occurring diseases under only image-level supervision, leaving disease-specific lesion attribution fundamentally under-constrained. Consequently, models may achieve correct predictions while relying on lesions from other co-occurring diseases. While Q2L extends transformer-based learning to multi-label classification, it does not explicitly address lesion–disease attribution ambiguity under disease co-occurrence. Our framework instead combines disease-specific patch reasoning with selective aggregation to encourage predictions to rely on disease-specific lesion evidence. 2.Performance gains and robustness (R2) We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding statistical variability across training runs. Nevertheless, the observed improvements show a consistent pattern across retinal imaging modalities. Importantly, the improvements are not limited to aggregate performance. As shown in Sec.3.4 and Fig.3, MD-PRSA consistently improves conditional AUC across co-occurring disease pairs, suggesting reduced reliance on spurious co-occurrence correlations and improved disease-specific reasoning. 3.Top-K selection (R1, R2, R3) The optimal K varies with disease morphology and imaging modality. As discussed in Sec.3.5, ODIR-5K contains diseases with distributed retinal manifestations, whereas LID-FFA mainly involves localized vascular abnormalities, naturally favoring different aggregation scales. This demonstrates that selective aggregation can adapt to disease spatial characteristics. This consideration is also discussed in the manuscript. 4.“first unified framework” claim (R2) We agree that the phrase “first unified framework” may be interpreted too broadly. We intended to highlight a key methodological distinction: prior methods, such as CABNet and other attention-guided approaches, primarily compute attention at the feature level, whereas our framework performs explicit disease-specific patch selection at the logit level through selective aggregation. We will revise the wording to avoid overstatement. 5.Dataset diversity and backbone selection (R2, R3) Our work specifically focuses on multi-disease retinal diagnosis, as reflected in the paper title. DenseNet121 was adopted to ensure fair comparison across all baselines and is widely used in retinal image analysis due to its parameter efficiency and stable optimization behavior. While broader evaluation across additional domains and architectures may further strengthen generalizability, the current experiments consistently support our central contribution in mitigating lesion–disease mismatching across diverse retinal imaging settings. (R3) The comparisons were also not limited to generic multi-label methods. Retinal-specific approaches such as Q2L Causal and MCAR were included under the same experimental setting. 6.Interpretability and computational cost (R1, R3) Fig.4 shows that the selected patches consistently correspond to clinically relevant lesion regions. In addition, the decoder operates on patch tokens, making the approach computationally practical.

title: Multi-probe Trait–State Latent Modeling for Cross-Context Clinical Motor Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem is relevant and important. The method effectively separates task-specific variations from stable subject traits and combines them for a consistent representation across clinical settings. The authors design four baselines to validate the approach. The results show improvements over the baselines and are promising. Figures 1 and 2 are clear and informative.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Section 2 needs to be reorganised. The current flow is hard to follow. The tokenization part can be better placed. The writing is too abstract and should be simplified for clarity. For D = 171, why are the remaining ~300 dimensions of \beta_s ignored? In the tokenization step, have you compared interleaving vs concatenation? What is their impact? Have you checked their individual contributions. The method description does not clearly explain the main contribution, i. e. , disentangling subject traits and task-specific motion. It also does not fully match the pipeline shown in Fig. 2.Part (a) of Fig. 2 is missing. It is also unclear where VQ-VAE is used in the figure. Overall, the figure is not self-explanatory. Why is Product-of-Experts (PoE) used for multi-probe aggregation? Also, why are three probes used per task? The metrics in Table 3 are not sufficient to support the disentanglement claim. Additional statistical or visual analysis of the learned feature distributions is needed. What is the theoretical and empirical justification for the claimed orthogonality between subject traits and task-specific latents in Section 2.2 (Eqs. 2 and 3)? What is the impact of not using resting-state gait in reconstruction? An ablation study is needed to support such design choices. A correlation of 0.6 with MAE of 0.38 may have limited clinical relevance. Please clarify. Also, explain what the 9 phenotypes represent. A clear table describing the baselines (input, method, output) would improve readability. A supplementary diagram of the pipelines can be helpful. Please correct a few spelling mistakes in some figures.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Capturing stable motor capacity across different tasks is important in clinical settings. The idea of separating a shared trait from task-specific effects makes sense and is very well motivated. The multi-center dataset and leave-one-center-out evaluation are a strong point and help with generalization. The evaluation looks at several aspects (descriptor fidelity, biomechanics, consistency), which is useful to address the feasibility of this approach..
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Similar disentanglement ideas have been explored before. 2.The model is evaluated via gait generation and correlation with descriptors, and it is not entirely clear how this translates to better clinical assessment. 3.It is still unclear what the learned “trait” actually represents in practice. The interpretation remains somewhat abstract in the text, it will be good to get better clarity on that. 4.The method is quite complex, and it is not fully clear which parts are really needed, since the ablation study is limited. 5.There is not much discussion about how robust the method is when tasks are noisy or not performed correctly.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clear practical motivation: Inferring a person’s stable motor capacity from several short standardized tasks instead of treating each task as a direct measure of ability as an underlying goal is relevant for clinical assessment. Large and representative dataset: A major strength is the dataset size and composition, especially the approximately balanced 50/50 male-female representation and the broad age range from 19 to 93 years. Appropriate evaluation framework: The paper uses generally suitable evaluation parameters, which supports the seriousness of the empirical setup. Ambitious methodological design: The work proposes a sophisticated latent modeling framework to represent motion and to separate subject-specific traits from context effects, which is methodologically ambitious and innovative. Modern modeling approach: The combination of body/joint tokenization with transformer-based modeling is a technically interesting choice and shows novelty in how motion is represented and analyzed.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Weak empirical support for the main claim: The reported correlation of around 0.60 seems too weak to convincingly support the paper’s central thesis about stable individual motor traits. Lack of statistical validation: The paper could provide more sufficient statistical analysis, such as significance testing or confidence intervals, to justify its conclusions. Insufficient interpretability of the mathematical formulation: The mathematical setup in my opinion is underexplained, particularly regarding the definition of variables and solution spaces, making it hard to judge whether the model is well-founded. Lack of explanation for key body coefficients and representations: The paper introduces body coefficients and joint-rotation representations without clearly explaining how these are determined or why they are appropriate. Poor writing and unclear phrasing: A major weakness is that the paper’s phrasing appears confusing, making even the main research question harder to understand than necessary.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the careful feedback. We address the main concerns on scope, novelty, clarity, tokenization, trait-state evidence, and robustness using only submitted results. Scope and empirical meaning (R1,R2,R5). Our goal is representation-level cross-context motor assessment, not diagnostic prediction. Standardized tasks are partial probes of a subject-level motor trait; gait synthesis is a held-out consistency probe decoded from z. Corr.=0.60 and MAE=0.38 measure fidelity to real-gait phenotype descriptors, not disease-classification accuracy. Under subject-disjoint 12-center LOCO, there is no target-center training, tuning, or leakage. With identical tokenizer, decoder, splits, and budget, our model improves over the strongest conditional baseline from 0.45 to 0.60 in Corr., 0.55 to 0.38 in MAE, and 0.52 to 0.72 in Top-1.The nine phenotypes are gait descriptors grouped into balance, strength, and rhythm. Novelty and method clarity (R1,R2,R5). We agree that disentanglement is a broad prior idea; our contribution is clinical multi-probe trait inference with z-only held-out gait validation, not generic disentanglement or generation. The path is: SMPL-X fitting; VQ-VAE tokenization of lower-body/trunk/global streams; transformer inference of per-probe z/u posteriors; PoE aggregation of z; and gait decoding from aggregated z. D=171 contains dynamic per-frame parameters only: 165 joint rotations, 3 root orientation, and 3 root translation. beta_s is a 300D static body-shape parameter used in fitting/reconstruction, not a frame-wise transformer input. The three probes are SLS, STS, and HK, not repeated trials. PoE uses posterior variance for precision-weighted aggregation and down-weights uncertain probes. Tokenization and concatenation (R1). The submitted “Concat (no latent)” baseline in Table 1 is a model-level baseline: it concatenates the three task probes and predicts gait without z/u factorization or PoE. It is not an isolated token-ordering ablation. Interleaving in Sec.2.3 serializes lower/trunk/global tokens frame by frame to preserve temporal alignment, while stream/time embeddings preserve component identity. Thus, the submitted evidence supports trait-state factorization with PoE over direct/concatenated conditioning, not interleaving itself as an independent contribution. Evidence for trait-state separation (R1,R2,R5). We use “separation” operationally, not as formal identifiability. The model imposes an informational bottleneck: task reconstruction uses z and u, whereas gait decoding accesses z but not u. Submitted Table 3 shows lower task prediction from our z than from corresponding Direct T→G/CondGen representations (0.27 vs. 0.61/0.57), high task prediction from u (0.92), and lower intra-subject z variance (0.035 vs. 0.083/0.072). These diagnostics do not prove statistical independence, but support reduced task leakage and more stable subject-level encoding. Resting gait, robustness, and reproducibility (R1,R2,R5). Resting gait is not excluded from training reconstruction: when available, Eq.9 includes gait-token reconstruction conditioned on z. What is withheld is using held-out gait as test-time input or conditioning; it is only the evaluation target. Eq.3 excludes u from the gait decoder to prevent task-specific transients from directly driving cross-context validation. Table 2 shows graceful degradation with fewer probes and reduced paired-gait supervision, addressing incomplete/noisy clinical observations. In every LOCO fold, held-out-center data are never used for tokenizer training, model fitting, or hyperparameter selection.

I’d encourage the authors to respond to key confusions raised by the reviewers, especially regarding subject-level traits and their disentanglement from task-level latents. | My opinion aligns more with R5.I think the study is novel and important and makes a great contribution. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the review concerns and author feedback, I am of the opinion that the clarifications provided have helped scope the contributions made by the work appropriately and am inclined to recommend acceptance. I find the overall approach sound and sufficiently motivated in terms of the application being considered. Their clarification of details from the paper during the rebuttal is helpful and addresses many review points raised. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This is an interesting work to learn a shared representation of a person’s motor traits by separating the task-specific movements from subject-specific traits. This can be then used to perform clinical motor assessment tasks. All the reviewers have agreed that this an important problem setting and the design makes sense and is intuitive. The baselines are well demonstrated with their corresponding technique gains also well justified. There were some issues raised regarding the theoretical motivation of the framework, however, the authors have tried to convincingly address those during their rebuttal. The major issue still pertinent with the paper is about the clarity and the organization of the paper with a better understanding so that the techniques and the framework could be implemented and reproducible. title: NutriDiff: Phenotype-Consistent Diffusion Augmentation for Malnutrition Screening
reviewer_1_strengths: The subject of elderly malnutrition screening via facial images is clinically relevant and underexplored. The paper introduces a clinically grounded filtering mechanism that enforces phenotype consistency in diffusion-generated samples, addressing label noise which is a known limitation in medical image synthesis. The authors propose a multi-view, view-conditioned LoRA adaptation strategy, enabling fine-grained control of facial pose and nutritional state without full model fine-tuning. The paper combines generative modeling with domain-specific feature engineering (ROI-based descriptors), which is relatively uncommon and well-motivated clinically. The method introduced demonstrates strong performance gains (e. g. , AUC 0.984, MCC 0.854) over both classical methods and diffusion-based baselines. The authors provide a systematic ablation study, clearly showing the impact of synthetic data and the necessity of phenotype filtering.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The evaluation suffers from a limited dataset size and single-center cohort (n=92) which reduces reliability and generalizability. There is no external validation dataset which is critical especially given domain shift (lighting, ethnicity, acquisition device). Lack of comparison with more recent controllable diffusion methods (e. g. , MedDiff-FT [Xie et al. , MICCAI 2025], VicTr [Susladkar et al. , ICCV 2025]) that explicitly address structural and clinical consistency. The phenotype descriptors are relatively simplistic (intensity ratios, Laplacian variance, gradients) and may not capture complex anatomical variations compared to learned feature-based approaches. The binary classification setting collapses malnutrition severity levels, limiting clinical usefulness compared to prior works considering richer stratification (e. g. , GLIM-based grading). Evaluation of synthetic image quality relies heavily on FID/AFFID, which are known to correlate poorly with clinical realism in medical imaging (as discussed in diffusion literature [Kazerouni et al. , 2023 survey]).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The use of diffusion models with phenotype-based filtering is a reasonable attempt to improve synthetic data quality. The integration with a downstream classifier shows empirical performance gains.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Misalignment with MICCAI Scope (Major Concern). The primary limitation of this work is that it is not well aligned with the core focus of MICCAI. The paper mainly focuses on facial image-based classification and diffusion-based data augmentation, which are more typical of the computer vision community (e.g., CVPR, ICCV, ECCV). The methodological contributions are centered around generative modeling and feature filtering rather than advancing medical imaging techniques, clinical workflows, or image-based diagnosis grounded in medical imaging modalities such as MRI, CT, or ultrasound. 2.Limited Medical Imaging Contribution. Although the application is related to healthcare (malnutrition screening), the method operates entirely on 2D facial photographs, which are closer to natural image processing rather than medical imaging. The paper does not leverage domain-specific medical imaging knowledge, physics, or clinically grounded modeling, which are central to MICCAI contributions. 3.Incremental Methodological Novelty. The technical contributions are largely incremental: Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion with LoRA is now standard practice. The phenotype filtering step is based on handcrafted features and Mahalanobis distance, which is relatively simple. 4.Weak Clinical Validation. The experiments are solely done with a private in-house dataset. 5.Limited Innovation in Diffusion Modeling. The paper does not propose a novel diffusion formulation but rather adapts existing Stable Diffusion models with conditioning and filtering. Compared to recent advances in medical diffusion models (e.g., structure-aware, physics-informed, or uncertainty-aware diffusion), the contribution is relatively limited.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The four facial ROIs (temporal, periorbital, malar, jawline) are grounded in established nutritional physiology and their use in the paper gives it strong clinical motivation. 2.The ablation study in Table 2 convincingly demonstrates that naive synthetic augmentation can degrade performance and their phenotypic filtering consistently improves all metrics 3.The multi-view design with subject-level score averaging is practical for bedside screening 4.Using separate LoRA adapters per view-class pair is a parameter-efficient strategy that avoids overfitting on the small dataset while capturing view-dependent morphological differences. 5.The paper is clearly written with a logical flow
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The dataset is extremely small and from a single center. this limits generalisability 2.No Cross Validation results 3.No statistical significance tests 4.There is domain shift between train (ambulatory patients) and test(bedridden ). This has not been analysed or discussed properly 5.No sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters such as 95th percentile Mahalanobis threshold, the generation multiplier β=8, and the synthetic loss weight γ=0.3.6.No standard augmentation baselines (geometric transforms, color jitter, CutMix, mixup) or non-diffusion generative methods (GANs, VAEs) are included 7.Individual components have limited novelty 8.Reproducibility : The dataset is private. No code release is mentioned
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their constructive comments and encouraging assessment of our manuscript. We appreciate their recognition of the clinical relevance and underexplored setting of elderly malnutrition screening (R1/R3), the phenotypic consistency filtering based on facial regions associated with nutritional status (R1/R3), the practical multi-view design (R3), and the empirical gains shown in the ablation study (R1/R3). To clarify the relevance to MICCAI and the work’s medical contribution (R2), our goal is not generic face generation. The paper investigates phenotype-consistent diffusion augmentation for elderly malnutrition screening. Facial images may capture phenotypic cues linked to nutritional status. This potential relevance to healthcare screening and geriatric assessment motivated our MICCAI submission. The filtering step uses facial ROIs tied to nutritional status to reduce mismatch in synthetic samples and to support an image-based clinical screening task. We agree with the reviewers that the small single-center cohort and the absence of external validation are important limitations (R1/R3). These limitations are partly due to the scarcity of data and prior work on facial image analysis for screening elderly malnutrition. To the best of our knowledge, no public dataset currently targets this task for individuals aged 65 years or older. We also clarify that the submitted test set includes bedridden patients and those receiving enteral nutrition, thereby providing an initial evaluation under more complex clinical conditions. For cross-validation and statistical rigor (R3), Table 2 in the submitted manuscript reports subject-level 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for ablation and stability analysis. These experiments compare real data, unfiltered synthetic augmentation, and phenotype-filtered synthetic augmentation across two backbones, with the mean and standard deviation reported. We agree that additional comparisons with traditional augmentation, GAN/VAE-based generation, and recent controllable diffusion methods would further strengthen the evaluation (R1/R3). Given the page limit and the focus of the study, the submitted experiments prioritize diffusion-based augmentation. The main objective is to assess whether phenotypic consistency filtering improves the clinical consistency and downstream screening utility of diffusion-generated samples. Broader comparisons across augmentation families will be an important direction for future work. We also appreciate the suggestions on hyperparameter sensitivity, landmark detection failure analysis, and t-SNE/UMAP visualization of real and synthetic feature distributions (R3). These analyses would provide useful evidence for understanding the generation and filtering process. Larger multi-center validation, more rigorous statistical and hyperparameter analyses, broader baseline comparisons, and external validation will be important extensions of this work. We again thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. Their comments will guide our future validation, broader comparisons, and continued clinical extension of this work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The reviews are generally positive, with two reviewers recommending weak acceptance and one reviewer recommending weak rejection. The paper addresses an underexplored and clinically relevant problem: facial-image-based malnutrition screening in elderly patients. I do not agree with the concern that the work is out of scope for MICCAI. Facial image diagnosis can be considered an important part of medical image analysis, with relevance to healthcare screening, geriatric assessment, and related areas such as AI-assisted facial analysis in healthcare and Traditional Chinese Medicine. The proposed diffusion-based augmentation framework, especially the phenotype-consistency filtering using clinically motivated facial regions, is well motivated and supported by ablation results. Given the positive overall assessment, clear clinical motivation, and empirical gains, I recommend early acceptance. However, several concerns raised by multiple reviewers should be addressed carefully in the final version, including the small single-center dataset, limited statistical rigor, absence of cross-validation or significance testing, lack of external validation, insufficient comparison with standard augmentation and recent generative baselines, and limited analysis of domain shift and hyperparameter sensitivity. The authors are strongly encouraged to clarify these issues, strengthen the discussion, and include recommended analyses where feasible so that the published work can have stronger impact.

title: OCS-MAMBA: Object-Centric, Logic-Guided Approach for Surgical Action Understanding
reviewer_1_strengths: The greatest strength of this paper is the integration of individual existing components in the creation of a solid systems. The factored Graph-Mamba design is particularly well-motivated and effective. Additionally, the RAG safety head is a meaningful step toward possible deployment making the work even more interesting. Ablation clearly show the contribution of the losses and how mamba improves long-horizon prediction, strengthening claims.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The manuscript could benefit by considering the following aspects: The is no formal analysis about Mamba working better than Transformers here. You should be doing a clear evaluation evaluating attention against Mamba and demonstrate how result are better or worse. This is something already shown in the field of animal action recognition (e. g, https://www. sciencedirect. com/science/article/pii/S1574954124004977) where authors shown that Mamba is indeed better than using Transformer (linear attention/transformer) and at the same time requiring less FLOPs and computational resources. You should do something similar, that would strengthen the method. The manuscript would benefit in a more extensive description of the RAG safety, I believe that is a very important component, especially in the surgery field. However, there is no well evaluation/description. Does it improve accuracy or only interpretability? Can you show real failure cases prevented? The limitations are described in a very short line in the conclusion section “Current constraints are tailored to cholecystectomy and require adaptation for other procedures, and the fixed slot budget may not generalise to scenes with more entity types. ”. The authors should try to understand what are possible limitations of the method and its usability and write a deeper analysis. This would improve the paper’s clarity and credibility. Finally, I feel like you give the spotlight to Mamba in your title, however DinoV2+slot attention does a huge amount of work in our framework. I would consider to reconsider the name for publication, like this is somewhat misleading and not completely honest. I would recommend to also test some other image backbone based on Mamba if you want to keep that title.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper is well organized and easy to follow. 2.The concept of utilizing object-centric knowledge has been proven beneficial for surgical workflow tasks but it is more helpful for fine-grained classification tasks. 3.The idea of using slots for tool-target together inherently allows to model interactions in the slot attention followed by factorized processing of spatial and temporal features aptly utilizing the long-term context. 4.The ontology loss idea used as a negative constraint acts as a regularizer and forces the model to adhere to allowed constraints. 5.The use of anticipation tasks together with triplet recognition mutually benefits both as reported in the results.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Slot Attention, famous in the unsupervised object discovery, generates slots that are unordered so the slots can bind to any object in the scene. How are the 21 queries handled to make sure that each query (e.g. grasper or gallbladder) correspond to the object segmentation mask of the same grasper or gallbladder. There is a mention of Presence predictor but does it mean each query is hardcoded to a specific class? Within the same paragraph Ot = ot,k is unclear and should have proper format. 2.The slots that are generated when visualized helps the readers to understand how the slot attention have captured the true object semantics - even though it is not perfect but it should roughly capture the parts of the instrument or anatomical structure to make more sense later in the graph message passing and the ontology constraints part. The lack of this information makes the manuscript a bit incomplete. 3.Overall, the manuscript should make it clear what it means by temporal. Is it short context e.g. 32/64 frames or is it all the frames of a video? 4.In the “Anticipation via State-Rollout” section, there seems to be a disconnect in the phrasing. First the future slots are mean pooled to get a single feature and then I, V, T are separately classified - does it mean no triplet head is present here? Then the manuscript mentions last-frame slots - last frame with reference to which group of frames? Is it a video clip with fewer frames? The manuscript will greatly benefit if these clarifications are properly provided. 5.The use of RAG guardrail - is it connected to the model training and/or evaluation pipeline? Because it is mentioned once before section 3, but not discussed later. The manuscript should provide clarification on this. 6.The implementation details regarding the value of feature dimension D, Mamba parameters, number of epochs or iterations, batch size, GPUs, etc. are missing which renders a big question on the reproducibility of the said experiments. 7.Minor weakness - Is there a rationale for choosing LSTM over autoregressive transformer for anticipation baselines?
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The three stage framework moves away from pixel-centric approach and decomposes video frames into discrete semantic entities and focuses on object-centric slots to explicitly track interactions between instruments and targets. The model is hence less prone to hallucinations and can reason about physical and procedural validity of actions The model enforces surgical safety through a semantic grammar and logic-constrained loss, directly penalizing physically impossible or unsafe instrument interactions. The addition of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) safety head provides interpretable guidance aligned with procedural guidelines, which is a significant step toward clinical feasibility and real-world deployment Evaluation on multiple public datasets supports the generalizability of the approach. The ablation studies further validates the effectiveness of each module, supporting claims of improved memory efficiency and safer predictions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Overall the paper is well-written and very clear. Some comments on weaknesses: The current approach in terms of logic constraints and ontological matrices for indicating mechanically invalid predictions are tailored to cholecystectomy. The authors acknowledges these constraints require adaptation for other surgical procedure. This thus limits the immediate applicability of the OCS-Mamba method to broader surgical domains The evaluation is conducted on public datasets such as CholecT50 and CholecSeg8k, thus it is not real how well the demonstration of clinical feasibility or deployment in real surgical environments.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We are delighted that our paper has been provisionally accepted and would like to sincerely thank the reviewers and the Meta-Reviewer for their thoughtful, relevant, and constructive feedback. We are especially pleased that the reviewers recognised the novelty and practical relevance of our object-centric methods. Reproducibility and Implementation Details (R2, Meta-Reviewer): We agree with the reviewers that some of the implementation details were missing. In the camera-ready version, we will clarify the key architectural and training settings. We also intend to make the source code and full configuration details available upon acceptance. Slot Attention Clarification (R2, Meta-Reviewer): We thank the reviewers for pointing out that the slot semantics require clearer explanation. The 21 slots are not manually hard-coded to specific classes. Rather, they are object-centric proposals whose semantics are learned through segmentation supervision, presence prediction, and IVT recognition losses. The presence predictor does not impose a fixed slot-to-class assignment, but encourages the slot set to represent relevant instruments and anatomical targets. We use Slot Attention as a structural inductive bias (object-like decomposition into K competing representations), but replace its unsupervised reconstruction objective entirely with task-specific surgical supervision. We will refine the description in the revision and also clarify the notation around $O_t$. Mamba Temporal Modelling (R1, Meta-Reviewer): Our motivation for adopting Mamba stemmed from the long procedural durations and dense temporal dependencies in surgical videos. Mamba offers linear complexity, efficient state propagation, and improved long-context scalability. The submitted experiments already include relevant Transformer/attention-based baselines, including FUTR, MT4MTL, TERL, and CurConMix. We clarify that OCS-Mamba does not simply replace Transformers with Mamba; DINOv2 remains the visual backbone, while Mamba is used within the factored Graph-Mamba stage for efficient temporal-state propagation over object-centric slot features. We will make this design motivation clearer in the camera-ready version. The title reflects the role of Mamba-based temporal reasoning within the broader object-centric and logic-guided framework. Anticipation Rollout and RAG Safety Module (R1, R2): Temporal modelling is performed over sequential frame groups rather than full videos simultaneously, where future slot states are recursively propagated before IVT decoding. We acknowledge that this section currently lacks sufficient clarity and will revise it accordingly. The RAG safety module is used only as an inference-time interpretability and procedural verification component. It is not used during training or optimisation and does not contribute to the reported performance metrics. Its role is to provide post-hoc safety-oriented feedback for predicted actions. A more extensive evaluation of RAG-guided safety verification, including clinical validation and failure-case analysis, remains important future work. Generalisability and Limitations (R1, R3): We acknowledge that the ontology constraints are currently tailored to cholecystectomy, the slot budget is fixed, and the evaluation is based on public datasets. These points, together with the need for prospective clinical validation before deployment, will be briefly emphasised in the discussion of future work and limitations.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): While two reviewers are strongly in favor of acceptance due to the framework’s impressive systems-level integration and innovative logic-guided constraints, R2 explicitly disagrees with a recommendation to reject. All reviewers recognize the paper’s strengths, specifically the effectiveness of the factored Graph-Mamba design for long-horizon prediction, the well-motivated use of object-centric slots, and the clinical potential of the RAG safety head for interpretable surgical guidance. However, there are concerns regarding a critical lack of implementation details—such as Mamba hyperparameters and feature dimensions—which severely hinders reproducibility. Furthermore, the authors must clarify the mechanics of the Slot Attention module regarding how unordered slots bind to specific semantic entities, provide a formal comparative analysis justifying the choice of Mamba over Transformer baselines, and offer a more robust evaluation of the RAG safety head’s ability to prevent real failure cases while discussing the limitations of generalizing these logic constraints beyond cholecystectomy.

title: OPVD: On-Policy Chain-of-Visual-Thought Distillation for Medical Reasoning
reviewer_1_strengths: This manuscript tackles key limitations of RL-based medical reasoning and proposes innovative CoVT mechanism. Strong empirical results.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Evaluation relies on single public dataset limiting generalizability claims. No compubation comparison (e. g. , FLOPs/samples versus RL baselines) No analysis of teacher quality or failure cases.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Since the teacher model is initialized from the same VLM, the oracle reasoning traces are closer to the student model’s distribution, enabling more guided learning. 2.The method outperforms bigger zero-shot models as well as other models trained using RL, setting a new state-of-the-art. 3.The paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Missing comparison with RL-based approaches: The paper states that OPVD significantly outperforms SFT and RL methods. Including comparisons with RL-optimized Qwen-VL models would help support this claim. 2.Framing and discussion: The claim that OPVD significantly outperforms RL methods is not clearly supported by the reported results (1–2% improvement). The comparison could be presented more conservatively. 3.Currently, the paper does not provide in-depth performance and failure analysis. It would be useful to include a) cases where OPVD outperforms SFT and b) where visual CoT outperforms text-only CoT.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: First, the paper addresses a relevant and timely problem in medical VLM reasoning, namely the inefficiency of RL-based training caused by sparse rewards and repeated sampling. The proposed use of token-level dense supervision through self-distillation is a meaningful conceptual contribution. Second, the method is clearly motivated and reasonably designed: the combination of privileged-answer teacher guidance, interleaved visual-text reasoning, and crop-and-zoom refinement is intuitive and well aligned with medical image understanding. Third, the empirical results are strong for the presented setup. OPVD consistently outperforms SFT baselines and also surpasses recent RL-based methods while requiring fewer sampling steps, which suggests a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff. Finally, the paper includes ablations on the visual reasoning component and the answer-weighting term, which helps support the importance of the proposed design choices.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the experimental validation is still relatively limited. The model is trained on only 2,000 MRI samples and evaluated on 900 samples across MRI, CT, and X-ray, which may not be sufficient to establish broad generalizability for medical reasoning. In addition, the comparison setting may not be fully controlled, since the paper states that the exact training splits of MedVLM-R1 were unavailable and the authors constructed their own subsets, making fairness of comparison somewhat uncertain. Another concern is that the teacher branch uses privileged ground-truth answers during trajectory construction, which is effective for training but also raises questions about how much of the improvement comes from richer supervision rather than improved reasoning alone. The paper would also benefit from more extensive analysis, such as additional benchmarks, more diverse modalities/tasks, stronger ablations, and evaluation beyond multiple-choice accuracy.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Rebuttal R1Q1 & R3Q1: Generalizability. We extended evaluation to the large-scale PMC-VQA dataset, including 227k samples, using Qwen2-VL-2B backbone. OPVD achieves a score of 48.7, consistently outperforming other competitors like Med-R1-2B (47.4) and MedVLM-R1-2B (47.5). Crucially, our main experiments train exclusively on MRI data while testing on CT and X-ray, demonstrating robust OOD generalization. This cross-modality and cross-benchmark consistency confirms that OPVD learns transferable, domain-agnostic reasoning patterns rather than overfitting to dataset-specific biases. R1Q2 & R2Q4: Computation and sampling num. Toward Qwen2-VL-2B as the base model, OPVD totally requires only ~0.5 EFLOPs during training, which is approximately 6× lower than the ~3.3 EFLOPs consumed by rule-based RL baselines. The ‘‘sampling num.’’ in Table 1 denotes forward times per training iteration. OPVD requires only 2 forward passes, whereas RL baselines need 4-16 rollouts. AC-Q1 & AC-Q2 & R1Q3 & R2Q3: Teacher quality and failure analysis. Teacher trajectories are validated via clinical priors, and Fig. 2 show the cases of the reliable reasoning process of OPVD. Failures mainly occur in complex OOD X-rays where pathologies are obscured, highlighting a need for future omni-modality training recipe. AC-Q1 & R2Q1: RL-based Qwen comparison. To ensure a strictly fair comparison, we fine-tuned Qwen2-VL-2B with GRPO under identical training budgets, data splits, learning rates, and batch configurations. Despite matched computational resources, the GRPO baseline achieves an average accuracy of 76.41, falling significantly short of OPVD’s 80.96.This gap stems from fundamental optimization differences: GRPO relies on sparse, answer-level rewards that provide weak gradient signals for intermediate steps, often leading to reward hacking. In contrast, OPVD’s token-level distillation directly aligns the student’s generative distribution with a clinically validated teacher trajectory at each decoding step, enabling precise, dense correction that is substantially more data-efficient and stable for medical reasoning. AC-Q1 & R2Q2: Conservative framing of gains. We will revise the claims to conservatively frame the 1-2% improvement in the manuscript. To rigorously validate reliability, we conducted paired statistical tests across multiple random seeds, yielding a p-value of 0.004, smaller than 0.01, when comparing OPVD against the strongest baseline (ViTAR), confirming the improvement is statistically significant rather than due to random variance. AC-Q1 & R3Q2: Fair comparison. To guarantee comparison fairness, we re-implemented and re-evaluated all cited baselines using a standardized protocol: identical train/validation/test splits, consistent image preprocessing, unified hyperparameter search spaces, and the same evaluation metrics and random seeds. Under these strictly controlled conditions, OPVD consistently maintains a performance advantage, reinforcing the reproducibility of our findings. AC-Q1 & R3Q3: Analysis on privileged prior. To isolate the impact of privileged priors, upon Qwen2-VL-2B, we trained standard SFT and RL baselines directly on the high-quality teacher-generated CoVT trajectories (i.e., using the same privileged reasoning paths as OPVD’s distillation targets). Despite access to identical prior knowledge, both baselines underperform significantly, achieving 64.29 (SFT) and 73.83 (RL) versus OPVD’s 80.96.This clear gap demonstrates that OPVD’s advantage does not stem merely from richer supervision, but from its dynamic on-policy distillation mechanism. R3Q4: Beyond MC accuracy and benchmarks. We plan to extend our research on report generation and more diverse benchmarks in future work. The interleaved CoVT architecture is inherently well-suited for these extensions, as it already produces structured, interpretable reasoning chains that can be seamlessly adapted to free-text generation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Although the three reviewers are rather positive about this paper, they raised some concerns about the experiment and evaluation design. As the meta-reviewer, I would like to see their responses to the following concerns: 1.Some of the reviewers have concerns about exps and results: the fairness of the comparison (different training split), the marginal improvement (1-2%), failure analysis, the ablation of richer supervision vas reasoning alone etc. 2.The evaluation pipeline seems to borrow a lot from the paper MedVLM-R1.It is acceptable for MedVLM-R1 to only evaluate on the final answer accuracy since it is one of the first works to carry out VLM reasoning. But since the field of reasoning has advanced significantly and the paper’s highlight is its CoVT, it is now also necessary to verify the intermediate process, i.e., whether the reasoning chain is plausible. | This paper has a clear motivation, while concerns of the comparison fairness and the evaluation pipeline are not well addressed, and the performance is still a bit too marginal. This paper is on the borderline. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers are consistently supportive of the paper. OPVD offers a practical alternative to RL-based medical reasoning through on-policy visual-thought distillation, and the empirical results are viewed positively. Some concerns about evaluation breadth and novelty remain, but they do not undermine the main contribution.

title: OR-Action: Multi-Role Video Understanding with Fine-Grained Actions
reviewer_1_strengths: External OR understanding is highly relevant and challenging due to occlusions, multi-actor interactions, and temporal complexity. OR-Action provides a new evaluation setting for fine-grained, multi-role temporal actions, which is valuable for the community. The paper highlights a significant gap between scene graph prediction and temporal action understanding. The vision-only model is simple, scalable, and benefits from strong pretrained video representations. The teacher–student alignment is relevant for real-world deployment where multi-view data is limited.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Evaluation unfairly disadvantages scene-graph approaches: The benchmark assesses scene-graph models using predicted graphs fed through a rule-mapping pipeline, which can lead to error propagation and misrepresent the limitations of the scene-graph paradigm. Comparisons with graph-based baselines are imbalanced: the vision model benefits from strong pretraining, whereas the graph-temporal baselines are simpler. The omission of stronger or hybrid alternatives weakens any comparative claims. Short temporal windows limit reasoning: Modelling only ≈16s fails to capture long-term procedural dependencies, restricting the ability to analyse complex OR actions. Errors and generalisation remain unexplored: The paper lacks per-class breakdown, detailed failure analysis, and robustness checks across roles or viewpoints.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The work provides a relevant benchmark that involves an extensive list of to-be-detected actions in a surgical scene. 2.It is shown convincingly that the sole use of exocentric camera views for detailed surgical action detection is very challenging, while egocentric views could improve the detection results. 3.The experiments show that good performance can be retained with a single egocentric view, using alignment by a student-teacher learning framework, and selecting the right clinical role (surgeon or assistant).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.An exhaustive list of action labels is not presented, which makes it more difficult to interpret the clinical relevance once these actions could be detected. 2.Instead of providing one qualitative example (Fig.3), it would be good to provide multiple examples with best and worst performances, to understand the full range of the method’s abilities.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Authors introduce multi-role OR benchmark for temporal action understanding enabling fine grained OR understanding. They demonstrate vision-only temporal model (VJEPA2-based) that significantly outperforms graph-based principled evaluation and a demo video. Paper is well written with apt set of experiments.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Annotation generation is heuristic and may encode “rule bias”, it is still not human verified. We can have some human in loop evaluation, like annotate random frames and evaluate. Multi-view OR / surgical action modeling exists in, e.g. Schmidt et al., 2021; clarify what is uniquely enabled by their alignment objective vs prior multi-view attention or distillation approaches.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and AC for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the relevance of OR-Action as a fine-grained multi-role benchmark for external OR understanding, as well as the practical value of egocentric video and multi-to-single-view alignment. Regarding the heuristic annotation pipeline and potential rule bias (R1/R3/R4), we agree this is an important limitation. Our goal is not to claim that rule-generated labels are equivalent to independently annotated human action labels. Rather, OR-Action is distilled from existing expert scene-graph annotations to enable the first temporal, role-specific evaluation on this public ego-exocentric OR dataset. We tried to make the actions as hard as possible, focusing on procedural aspects that are hard to distinguish without longer temporal context to provide an interesting avenue for future research. Our results for both vision only and even oracle GT+GNN models highlight that current models are not yet equipped to fully handle multi-view multi-actor video understanding, with relatively low Edit and F1 scores compared to easier datasets. Regarding fairness to scene-graph methods and the GNN baseline (R1/R4), we will clarify that the predicted-scene-graph results should not be read as a rejection of scene graphs as a paradigm. Our GT+GNN upper bound shows that ground-truth scene graphs are informative for action understanding; the main gap is between predicted frame-wise graphs and temporally coherent dense actions. We will try to include the GNN implementation and training details in the official benchmark release. Regarding the vision model, temporal context, and baseline comparisons (R1/R4), our intent is to evaluate whether strong pretrained video representations with explicit temporal pooling can form an effective alternative to predicted scene graphs in this benchmark. The 64-frame / 16s window was chosen to match the video encoder setting and keep the method deployable in streaming OR scenarios. We agree that longer context may capture procedural dependencies beyond local actions, but want to clarify that running video encoders such as VJEPA2 on clips much longer than 16 seconds becomes computationally infeasible due to quadratic self-attention scaling. Regarding multi-to-single-view alignment (R1/R3/R4), we agree that the presentation should better separate what is demonstrated from what remains a hypothesis. The results show that a single-view student can improve when aligned to a multi-view teacher, especially for clinically active viewpoints such as surgeon and assistant. We will clarify claims that the student “sees” unobserved viewpoints and instead describe the objective as distilling multi-view contextual structure when cues are present in the observed stream. Regarding technical clarity (R4), we will clarify that idle is handled through the separate activity head, while the fine-grained action head is evaluated on active frames after masking. We will also clarify how temporal tokens are obtained by setting the Role Pooler query count to the number of sampled frames and supervising the sequence frame-wise, simplify notation such as R_in, fix the missing Fig. 1 reference. We reaffirm that the code and annotations will be made public upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces a fine-grained multi-role action-centric benchmark for operating room video understanding derived from an existing dataset, together with a vision-only temporal model and a cross-view feature alignment strategy. Reviewers highlight the relevance of a fine-grained benchmark, the convincing demonstration of the vision-only temporal models, and the practical utility of the alignment scheme. Reviewers raise concerns about potential rule-bias in the heuristic annotation pipeline, limited graph-based baselines, short temporal context windows, missing per-class and failure analyses, etc. Reviews are consistent in supporting acceptance.

title: Ordinal Diffusion Models for Color Fundus Images
reviewer_1_strengths: The approach is simple and effective. Especially Figure 4 showcases that the ordinal labels are really doing what they are supposed to be doing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are other diffusion models working with ordinal labels, e. g. Cho et al. “Conditional Diffusion with Ordinal Regression: Longitudinal Data Generation for Neurodegenerative Disease Studies” ICLR 2025 – https://github. com/Hannah37/ConDOR-ICLR25 weakening the claim “our model is the first reproducible ordinal diffusion model to explicitly encode ordinal and structural constraints” I am not sure, why learned margins are included as they provide little benefit even over the baseline and perform consistently worse than equidistant margins. However, apart from this the method section is largely a rehash of existing methods. The section on Ordinal Disease stage conditioning, which is the novel part of the paper is just 3 sentences. Complete absence of any baselines. There should be at least a GAN based one, as StyleGANs have been used for such conditional generation for quite a while now. The images are significantly downscaled and hence unsuitable for downstream training, as the resolution is just 256x256. Furthermore, the vessel structure is not retained in the generated images, e. g. there is additional branching and closing of the vessels. However, this is never commented on. The writing is also not ideal. The first sentence of the abstract starts with “It has been suggested” –> either someone claimed this and then cite the paper or do not mention this.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1.Strong evaluation: The paper presents a thorough experimental design, evaluating six independently trained model variants. S2.Novelty of the combined approach: The combination of ordinal disease-grade conditioning with structure-preserving conditioning is, to the best of this reviewer’s knowledge, novel in the context of diffusion-based medical image generation. The ordinal encodings (equidistant and learned margins) are well-motivated and provide a principled way to exploit the ordered nature of DR severity. S3.Clear improvement over baseline: The equidistant margins model with structural conditioning shows consistent FID and QWK improvements. S4.Reproducibility: The authors provide clean code and model weights. S5.Extendability: The proposed approach is not specific to DR or fundus imaging and could be applied to other medical domains with ordinal severity grading (e.g., cancer staging), which broadens the potential impact of the work. S6.Additional validation experiments: The interpolation and counterfactual generation experiments go beyond standard FID/QWK evaluation and attempt to demonstrate that the model captures a continuous disease spectrum, which strengthens the paper’s narrative (though see C2 and C3 regarding their execution).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.Dataset reproducibility gap: The authors report using 127,144 images from EyePACS after quality filtering, but cite only the original 2009 system description paper. The publicly available versions of this dataset (e.g., https://www.kaggle.com/c/diabetic-retinopathy-detection) contain around 35k labelled samples. For reproducibility, the authors should clarify which version was used, how it can be accessed, and provide the per-class distribution after filtering. W2.FID methodology unclear for minority classes: The authors state that FID was computed between 10,000 real and 10,000 generated images per DR grade. However, the publicly available version has fewer than 1000 samples per stage 3 and 4.Even with the author’s larger 127,144-image version of EyePACS, it seems unlikely that these stages have 10,000 samples each. The authors should clarify how FID was computed for these minority classes. W3.Unfair characterisation of prior work: The paper claims to be the ‘first reproducible ordinal diffusion model to explicitly encode ordinal and structural constraints.’ While the structural conditioning component is novel, the discussion of prior ordinal diffusion work is not entirely fair. Reference [29] is described as not consistently yielding better performance in terms of realism, yet their reported results show improved FID over the standard diffusion baseline on both evaluated datasets. Reference [17]’s Additive Ordinal Embedder enforces ordinal structure through cumulative summation, which is conceptually similar to the learned margins proposed in this paper - dismissing it as having ‘no constraints enforced’ misrepresents that work. The authors are encouraged to more accurately acknowledge prior work. W4.Baseline classifier performance not reported: The QWK is computed using a pretrained DR classifier, and the authors note that this classifier performed better on generated images than on real data. However, the baseline classifier performance on real images is not reported, making it difficult to contextualise the QWK results. This also raises the question of whether the generated images capture the full diversity of real pathology or tend toward more prototypical examples.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically motivated and clearly articulated problem: Modeling disease severity as a continuum rather than discrete categories is a genuine and well-reasoned contribution, particularly relevant for DR where progression is inherently gradual. 2.Simple yet effective design: The ordinal encoding (especially equidistant margins) is minimal and elegant, adding little complexity over baseline while yielding consistent improvements (QWK: 0.79→0.87). 3.Reproducible: Code is publicly available (anonymized link provided), and the full configuration is described. This is a significant plus. 4.Interpolation experiment: The interpolation analysis (Figure 4) is scientifically interesting and provides strong evidence that the model has learned a continuous disease manifold, not just discrete clusters. 5.Honest evaluation: The paper candidly acknowledges that the DR classifier performed better on generated images than real ones, suggesting possible dataset label noise, which is a thoughtful and credible observation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited resolution (256×256): Fundus images at this resolution miss fine-grained pathological details (microaneurysms, small hemorrhages). The paper acknowledges this but does not provide experiments at higher resolutions, which is a significant limitation for clinical utility. 2.Learned margins did not consistently outperform equidistant: Despite their theoretical appeal, learned margins performed worse on several metrics. The paper lacks a deeper analysis of why this is the case. 3.No human/expert evaluation: The evaluation is entirely automated (FID + classifier). Clinical utility of generated images requires ophthalmologist assessment, which is explicitly deferred to future work. 4.Structural encoder generalization: The structural encoder is trained on EyePACS (same distribution). Its behavior under domain shift is not evaluated. 5.Proliferative DR generation is poor (FID=38 with equidistant, structural cond.), likely due to class imbalance. The mitigations beyond weighted sampling are not explored.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Our core contributions - explicit ordinal encoding of disease severity and dual conditioning - were recognized as simple yet effective, novel, and broadly applicable. The interpolation analysis further demonstrated that the model captures a continuous disease spectrum, directly supporting our central design goal. We emphasize that our focus is on ordinal conditioning, where our approach consistently improves the baseline across metrics rather than on generating optimal fundus images. 1.Novelty relative to prior work (R1, R2) ConDOR (Cho et al.) uses ordinal regression to predict disease stage from image features and age, whereas we use the grade label directly as a geometrically structured conditioning representation. ConDOR also targets subject-level trajectories from paired longitudinal data; we address cohort-level generation from cross-sectional data. Both support continuous interpolation, but along different axes: ConDOR along time, ours along disease severity. [29] and [17] impose ordinal structure implicitly - via regularization on image differences and a high-dimensional learned embedding (768-d) - encouraging but not guaranteeing ordinality. We impose it explicitly on a scalar axis, defining an ordinal scale by construction. Notably, [29] does not consistently improve across all DR grades (Fig. 4). We will narrow our claim to: “To our knowledge, this is the first reproducible work to explicitly encode ordinal geometric constraints into the conditioning representation of a latent diffusion model for disease staging.” 2.Dataset (R2) We used the licensed EyePACS dataset (accessed 2022), larger than the public Kaggle subset (~35k images). Since our method requires only DR grade labels, Kaggle offers a reproducible starting point. Class distribution after quality filtering: Grade 0: 100,584; Grade 1: 9,948; Grade 2: 14,823; Grade 3: 960; Grade 4: 829 (N=127,144). 3.Minority class FID computation (R2) FID is highly sensitive to small sample sizes, making class-specific comparisons infeasible. We therefore computed FID using a fixed reference pool of 10,000 randomly sampled real images from the full set and compared against 10,000 generated images from each class. Class-specific feature fidelity was assessed with a DR classifier. We will clarify this in the final version. 4.Stronger baselines (R1) Our core claim is that ordinal conditioning improves over categorical conditioning, not that diffusion models outperform GANs. Our categorical diffusion baseline isolates this by keeping the architecture fixed, ensuring any performance difference is attributable to the architecture-agnostic conditioning alone. 5.Clinical limitations (R1, R3) Ordinal conditioning is resolution-agnostic and directly applicable to higher-resolution LDMs. Expert evaluation and higher resolution are planned next steps. 6.Failure modes (R1, R3) Discussion of vessel structure limitations will be added. Class imbalance is likely the primary driver of higher minority-class FIDs; sampling strategies are a promising future direction. 7.Learned margins (R1-R3) Learned margins make no assumptions about inter-stage distances, allowing the model to learn inter-stage geometry from data, but may suffer from training instability due to the additional learnable parameters and insufficient gradient signal from minority classes. While performing on par with the baseline, they provide improved interpretability through clinically meaningful margins. We will clarify this in the final version. 8.Misc. We will: optimize the abstract (R1); report baseline classifier performance, expand the Fig. 1 caption, and improve Fig. 4 with clearer labels, an explicit text reference, and a note that interpolation analysis is impossible with the categorical baseline (R2). Future directions include quantitative evaluation of counterfactual images via FID/QWK (R2) and latent space analysis for potential bias in the structural encoder (R3).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes an ordinal latent diffusion model for color fundus image generation, using ordinal disease-stage conditioning and structural conditioning to better reflect the progressive nature of DR. Reviewers appreciated the simplicity of the approach, the reproducibility/code availability, and the interpolation analysis suggesting a continuous disease spectrum. However, the reviews are mixed and raise important concerns. The main issues are the limited methodological novelty, incomplete positioning with respect to prior ordinal diffusion models, lack of stronger generative baselines, and unclear dataset/evaluation details, particularly the EyePACS version and FID computation for minority classes. Reviewers also noted limited clinical utility due to low image resolution, lack of expert evaluation, poor generation for severe DR, and insufficient analysis of why learned margins underperform equidistant margins. The authors should address: 1- Novelty and positioning relative to prior ordinal diffusion work. 2- Dataset version, class distribution, and access details. 3- FID computation for minority DR classes. 4- Absence of stronger generative baselines. 5- Clinical limitations from 256×256 resolution and lack of expert evaluation. 6- Failure modes, especially vessel artifacts and poor severe-DR generation. 7- Why learned margins underperform equidistant margins. | In the rebuttal, the authors addressed the main concerns reasonably well. In particular, they clarified the EyePACS dataset version and access conditions, explained the class distribution and the protocol used for FID computation in minority classes, and moderated the novelty claims relative to prior ordinal diffusion work. These clarifications resolve some of the main reproducibility and evaluation ambiguities raised in the reviews. The paper still has limitations. The methodological novelty remains moderate, the comparison to stronger generative baselines could be more complete, and the clinical usefulness of the generated images is still constrained by the 256×256 resolution and the lack of expert evaluation. In addition, severe DR generation remains more challenging, and the learned-margin variant is less convincing than the equidistant formulation. That said, the work is technically sound, reproducible, and provides a meaningful contribution in a relevant and emerging direction.
