title: TopoOR: A Unified Topological Scene Representation for the Operating Room
reviewer_1_strengths: Higher-Order Expressivity: The shift from dyadic (pairwise) to polyadic (group-based) modeling is a major contribution. By using Combinatorial Complexes, the model can represent complex group interactions (e. g. , a surgeon, an assistant, and a robotic tool working in unison) as a single mathematical unit. Avoidance of Latent “Averaging”: The paper introduces a higher-order attention mechanism that keeps different data types (3D poses, audio, robot kinematics) distinct rather than forcing them into a single, shared latent representation. This ensures that modality-specific details aren’t “washed out” during the fusion process. Hierarchical Reasoning: The architecture allows information to flow through different “ranks” of cells (from individual objects to small groups to large teams). Theoretical Grounding: The paper provides a formal mathematical bridge between Topological Deep Learning and Surgical Scene Graphs.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Data Sparsity and Statistical Significance of Higher-Order Relations The manuscript proposes a highly sophisticated topological model for the surgical environment. A primary concern lies in the data requirements for such a framework. While the MN-OR dataset is currently the most comprehensive for this task , it may still be insufficient to validate a polyadic approach. In a standard dyadic model, pairwise events occur frequently enough to provide statistical robustness. However, as the model moves toward higher-order Combinatorial Complexes, the number of unique combinations increases while the number of occurrences per combination naturally decreases. I am concerned that the “long tail” of complex group interactions in this dataset is too sparse to truly evaluate the performance and generalization of the proposed higher-order attention mechanism. 2.Breadth of Evaluation The evaluation is currently limited to a single dataset. While this might be the only relevant dataset, this singular focus limits the validation of the model’s robustness across different surgical specialties or OR configurations. Furthermore, the overall quantitative evaluation appears to be based on a limited number of test cases, which may not fully capture the model’s reliability in edge-case safety scenarios. 3.Automated vs. Manual Hierarchy Construction The methodology behind the “lifting” process requires further clarification. It is not entirely clear if the higher-order combinations (the $k$-cells) are generated fully automatically through spatial/temporal heuristics, or if there was manual intervention involved in selecting which specific hierarchies to prioritize. 4.Supplemental Material and Qualitative Evidence While the supplemental video is visually impressive, its contribution to the scientific validation of the model is unclear. I would appreciate it if the authors could provide more information on it.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The mathematical background of the method is clearly explained. 2.Ablations in Tab.3 clearly show the merits of the proposed frameworks in handling various modalities. 3.Overall the work is novel and has sufficient ablations to support the merits.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: As such there are no significant drawbacks but few issues need to be addressed to maintain the scientific standards. The details are provided in the additional comments section along with few suggestions related to the work.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The presented approach brings technical novelty while achieving state-of-the-art performance in next action prediction and robot phase recognition. 2.The ablations show how the method utilizes all input modalities for improved estimations, including the introduction of temporal edges.

Comparison with a wider variety of methods, reporting of multiple metrics, scores per class, and standard deviations will make it easier to interpret the impact of the presented results. 2.While a limitation is discussed that addresses surgical scene understanding benchmarks, it would be good to discuss/show the limitations of the presented method as well. 3.For example, it seems that the method requires priors by predefined domain-specific instances and relations. To get the full picture on the applicability of the method, I think it would be good to elaborate on the potential challenges that this poses.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive comments and respond to the main points below. Statistical capacity (R1, W1): We agree that sparse higher-order events are a central challenge in OR modeling. Our construction is designed to mitigate this issue by using higher-order structure as an inductive bias rather than treating every polyadic tuple as an independent class. This is particularly important in low-data regimes: known geometric and clinical priors constrain the hypothesis space, preserve modality-specific structure, and reduce the need to relearn domain relations purely from data. In HAT, the projections W_Q, W_K, and W_V are shared across cells of all ranks; only a small learnable rank-pair bias, b_{rk(y),rk(x)}, modulates source-target routing. Capacity, therefore, scales with the number of cell instances seen in training, not with the count of unique polyadic combinations. Cell construction (R1, W3): Per §2.3, all k-cells are produced deterministically from a small, fixed rule set: kinematic trees for intra-entity skeleton edges, a spatial-proximity threshold for inter-entity edges, and a compact list of domain-specific semantic links (e.g., Technician-Robot). No per-scene or per-sample manual intervention is involved. Sterility-breach parity (R2, c1): We agree with R2 that sterility breaches primarily depend on spatial proximity and therefore do not require the full higher-order hierarchy. As stated in §2.4, sterility breach is computed by “rule-based spatial heuristics directly over the 3D entities,” not by a learned task head. All 3D-grounded methods, therefore, share the same evaluation and produce identical scores; the parity reflects the evaluation protocol. Per R2’s comment 2, a per-rank ablation isolating each rank’s contribution per task is a valuable direction for extended work. Method limitations and prior dependence (R4, W2-W3): Beyond the dataset constraints, the principal methodological limitation is dependence on upstream perception (pose, depth, segmentation); errors there propagate into the cell structure. This constraint will ease as OR perception models improve. The proximity threshold can be replaced by a learnable soft kernel with no architectural change. The semantic-link prior is small and intentional, but new procedures (e.g., laparoscopy: endoscope/tissue, tool/tool, surgeon/console) require re-specifying the link set. We will expand the Limitations section accordingly. Evaluation breadth (R4, W1; R1, W2): Cross-institution and cross-procedure validation is important. MM-OR, however, is currently the only multimodal OR benchmark at this scope, and we follow the Macro-F1 protocol of [20] for a like-for-like comparison with the MM2SG baseline, which itself does not report per-class scores. Within that constraint, Tab. 3 isolates each modality’s contribution, and the three tasks cover spatial safety, current-state recognition, and temporal anticipation. Cross-procedure validation remains a key direction as comprehensive OR datasets emerge. Supplemental video (R1, W4): The video visualizes the constructed combinatorial complex on a single time frame: 3D bounding boxes, human skeletons, and rank-1/rank-2 cells rendered as edges and faces. It conveys the explicit hierarchical structure on which the model operates, which is difficult to view from static images. Writing and notation (R2, c3-5): The notation in Eqs. 1-3 combines standard topological deep learning conventions for cells, ranks, and incidence neighborhoods with standard query-key-value attention. On punctuation, we use em dashes primarily for appositive or parenthetical clauses, though we will reduce nonessential instances in the camera-ready version. To keep the MICCAI revision focused, we retain the current figure layout and will consider R2’s restructuring suggestions in a subsequent journal extension.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents TopoOR, a framework for surgical scene understanding that models higher‑order, polyadic interactions in the operating room using Combinatorial Complexes and higher‑order attention over multimodal signals. Reviewers agree that the approach is novel and well grounded, noting that it meaningfully advances beyond traditional dyadic scene representations and enables hierarchical reasoning across multiple relational ranks. Empirical results and ablations indicate that leveraging higher‑order structure and multimodal information improves performance on several downstream tasks. Reviewers also point out limitations, including evaluation on a single, sparse benchmark, relatively limited quantitative breadth, and the need for clearer exposition of how higher‑order relations are constructed and what assumptions they impose. Nonetheless, these constraints are largely attributed to current data availability rather than deficiencies in the proposed formulation, and the work is regarded as a strong contribution to surgical scene modelling.

title: Toward Markerless Video-Based Tremor Analysis: Objective Quantification of Pathological Tremor in Mouse Preclinical Models
reviewer_1_strengths: The suggested framework largely improves current camera-based tremor identification accuracy to be comparable with accelerometer data. The framework is non-invasisive, cost-efficient, and requires only little manual labor.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper does not mention any limitations of their proposed framework, e. g. how does the camera frame rate and lighting affect the pose estimation accuracy and subsequent pipeline. Could additional cameras further improve the accuracy? How does accelerometer data compare to other motion capture data? The paper does not provide any information on ethics approval for the data collection.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important preclinical problem: tremor quantification without invasive sensors, specifically in mice. The problem formulation is also well defined, as the 2 concrete technical challenges are depicted: separating tremor from voluntary locomotion and capturing anti-gravity tremor that may be missed from top-down views. The authors provide implementation details in section 3, but they could be more complete to promote reproducibility. The evaluation is plausible, with minimal proof of concept (as depicted in Table 1). The paper compares against accelerometer PSD, compares with human subjective scoring, includes ablations, and includes a threshold sensitivity analysis. Also, the harmaline dose-response analysis is a meaningful validation, since the method is not only correlated with the sensor signal, but also tracks an expected biological effect, which increases confidence in the score.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The system combines existing ingredients, including SAM 2 for segmentation, DeepLabCut for pose estimation, confidence-based view selection, thresholded movement filtering, and peak prominence scoring. The contribution is useful and well-engineered, but the conceptual advance over prior art feels incremental over Ajima et al. for objective microtremor detection and Ni et al. for motion and tremor tracking. The dataset is relatively limited, comprising 56 sequences from 28 mice collected in a single experimental setup. The manuscript also does not clearly specify whether the thresholds were tuned using held-out animals, making it difficult to assess the risk of overfitting. As a result, the extent to which the method generalizes across sessions, acquisition setups, and posture variations remains unclear. In addition, the subjective evaluation appears to rely on only one experienced evaluator. A stronger analysis of rater consistency would make the comparison with human assessment more convincing. The statistical reporting is somewhat limited. Correlation and one-way ANOVA are useful, but confidence intervals, significance testing between methods, and more detailed error analysis would strengthen the claims.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The pipeline is straightforward. Filtering out irrelevant data points by thresholding can improve the precision of the downstream task. 2.The manuscript is easy to understand and practically addresses the tremor monitoring problem.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The authors use wording that may imply that a new module is introduced (e.g., “the proposed method introduces a segmentation module”). However, this segmentation module is essentially a combination of SAM2, DeepLabCut, and thresholding. The authors should consider using different wording in this case. 2.The authors rely on head position movement (x, y) throughout the entire pipeline (for both filtering and tremor detection). However, the depth dimension is completely omitted, even though the mouse moves in 3D space. 3.While hyperparameter studies are provided for the two thresholds, it would be better to provide the corresponding data distributions to justify the selected ranges for the ablation studies. 4.It would be more precise to define the thresholds in physical units (e.g., cm or mm) rather than pixels. Using pixels makes the algorithm difficult to reproduce, since different cameras have different intrinsic parameters. 5.Please justify why PSD can be assumed to accurately capture tremor characteristics and therefore serve as ground truth. It is also unclear why human evaluation shows lower correlation than the proposed method. It would be helpful to discuss cases missed by human evaluation, or whether some cases are false positives from PSD and the proposed method. 6.The baseline setting is somewhat questionable. Ni et al. use an overhead view and track the animal’s center, whereas the authors use a side view while also tracking the animal’s center. Since tracking is performed in different planes, it is unclear whether it is fair to conclude that Ni et al. does not work in this new setting. 7.All module ablation studies show only minimal performance decreases. For example, without the multi-view setting, the correlation is still 0.82.Does this imply that pose estimation still works well in the back view despite self-occlusion? Similarly, without the movement detection module, the correlation remains 0.78.Does this suggest that detecting subtle movement is not particularly necessary? It would also be useful to provide implementation details for each ablation setting. 8.The authors claim that segmentation with SAM2 is necessary based on their ablation study. However, this may simply reflect limitations of DeepLabCut tracking. Could SAM2 be omitted if a stronger pose estimation model were used, or if the pose estimator were trained with more data?
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We are pleased that the reviewers recognized the potential and practical significance of our work, including its “high translational impact” (R1), a “meaningful problem” with “encouraging validation against accelerometer data” (R2), and its “practical value” (R3). We address primary concerns below. 1.GT Justification and Method Limitations (R1, R3): Accelerometer PSD is validated as a preclinical standard [4]. Marker-based capture [11] requires implantation, making it incompatible with our non-invasive premise. Lighting robustness was verified across conditions, maintaining r≈0.8 even under reduced brightness. 2.Novelty (R2): Our novelty lies in the problem formulation itself. No prior framework has addressed markerless, non-invasive quantification of anti-gravity tremor in freely moving mice. To solve this, we proposed two novel components absent from prior work: the Move Detection Module and prominence-based Tremor Score Estimation. Prior work either requires specialized piezoelectric sensors [1] or fundamentally fails because overhead tracking cannot capture anti-gravity vertical head oscillation [16]. In contrast, our method achieves dose-dependent replication (Figs. 3, 4), satisfying the application impact criterion under MICCAI’s joint evaluation framework. 3.Limited Dataset (R2, R3): Our dataset with n=28 (56 sequences) meets or exceeds those of prior work [1, 4, 16] (n=36, 11, 9), noting prior work [4] also uses a single fixed configuration. Thresholds were set on a held-out pilot subset, and Fig. 2 confirms wide-range stability. 4.Human Evaluation (R2, R3): Please note that human evaluation serves only as a supplementary reference, since human evaluators tend to anchor on peak intensity and overscore subsiding tremor sequences, whereas our method avoids this bias. Our primary claim is the strong correlation between our tremor score and accelerometer PSD (r=0.86). We acknowledge the single-rater limitation and plan to conduct multi-rater analysis. 5.Additional Statistical Report (R2): These details were omitted due to space. 95% bootstrap CIs (Fig. 4): SAL 10.2 [6.0, 14.5]; 5 mg/kg 27.9 [15.3, 46.4]; 10 mg/kg 58.7 [32.9, 83.4]; 20 mg/kg 75.1 [55.1, 95.0]. Non-overlapping CIs between SAL and 5mg/kg confirm lowest-dose discrimination. For r=0.86 (n=28): 95% CI≈[0.72, 0.93] (Fisher’s z). Our method is significantly superior to the baseline [16] (p<0.001). The difference vs. human (r=0.82, p≈0.63) is non-significant, confirming comparable accuracy. 6.Reproducibility and Threshold Guidelines (R3): Our recording uses 1280×720 resolution at a camera-to-subject distance that yields 1px = 0.2mm. Since this ratio depends on camera-to-subject distance for a fixed lens, it can be re-established by placing a known-size reference object in the field of view. Full setup details will be stated in the camera-ready version, with code released upon acceptance. Thresholds were not set arbitrarily but grounded in the observed data structure, as pilot experiments revealed bimodal prominence distributions with a natural valley, and both thresholds were placed at this valley. 7.Comparison Fairness with Methods Using Different Viewpoints (R3): Prior work [16] adopts an overhead view designed for tracking general locomotion, which fundamentally cannot capture the primary tremor phenomenon. Harmaline tremor manifests as anti-gravity vertical head oscillation (Fig. 5), which is inherently invisible from a top-down viewpoint. The result of r=−0.27 also supports this. 8.Ablation Study (R3): Without the Move Detection Module, vigorous locomotion contaminates tremor scores at low doses. Without SAM2 masking the background, DLC misidentifies cage elements as keypoints regardless of pose estimator strength. Multi-view ablation (r=0.82 without back camera) confirms complementary contribution. 9.Misc. (R1, R2, R3): Ethics approval and all minor corrections (Fig. 1, segmentation wording, typos, notations) will be reflected in the camera-ready.

However, reviewers raised concerns regarding the methodological novelty expected for a MIC-track contribution. The methodology-wise novelty seems limited, as the pipeline appears to be an engineering design that concatenates multiple existing components (e.g., SAM2, DeepLabCut, threshold-based filtering, and prominence-based scoring) into an application-specific framework, and the conceptual advance over prior work was viewed as incremental. While the rebuttal clarified several implementation and evaluation details, it did not substantially change this concern. One of the reviewers suggested acceptance under the “Clinical Translation” track with an “Application” contribution since the work is motivated by potential translational relevance. title: TRACE-PSG: Traceable Sleep Diagnosis Support with Pointer-Grounded Evidence
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem. Many recent multimodal medical LLM papers focus on general question answering or report generation, but fewer address auditable decision support on dense clinical documents where explicit evidence localization matters. The focus on grounding and traceability is therefore timely and clinically relevant. A major strength is the task formulation. Instead of relying on unconstrained free-text generation, the paper uses structured JSON outputs with pointerized evidence atoms. This makes the system more checkable and clinically accountable, and the distinction between syntactic validity and factual grounding is well made. The two-stage design is also sensible. Teaching the model to read and extract report content before full structured generation appears principled, and the ablations suggest that this alignment stage contributes meaningfully to parsing, grounding, and diagnostic behavior. I also appreciate the evaluation design. The paper reports not only end-task prediction performance, but also parseability, pointer validity, grounding, safety-oriented overdiagnosis behavior, and clinician rubric scores. This broader evaluation is better aligned with deployment concerns than using a single accuracy metric alone. Overall, the paper feels reasonably novel in the way it combines multimodal document reading, explicit provenance constraints, bounded evidence, and abstention-aware evaluation for sleep-report decision support.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My main concern is that the baseline section is somewhat narrow. The paper compares mainly against Qwen3-VL variants, which are useful foundation-model references, but not necessarily the strongest comparison set for a paper centered on grounding and auditable decision support. Stronger grounding-oriented or verification-oriented baselines would better contextualize the contribution. A second issue is that some of the strongest gains are on verifiability metrics that are partly induced by the design itself. The Pointer Bank and bounded evidence budget naturally improve parseability and grounding-pass behavior. That is still valuable, but these improvements should be interpreted primarily as gains in controllability and auditability rather than broad evidence of superior clinical reasoning across all output types. The clinical evaluation is also still limited. The clinician rubric is useful, but it is based on 100 cases and appears to show only modest separation among systems, especially for the longer-form recommendation content. This makes it harder to judge how large the practical downstream benefit is beyond the structured, verifiable fields. Another limitation is generalization. The dataset comes from a single tertiary sleep center, is insomnia-dominant, and may reflect site-specific reporting conventions. The paper acknowledges this, but the question of portability to other institutions and report templates remains open. Finally, some methodological details would benefit from stronger justification. In particular, the choice of beta equals zero in the GRPO stage raises questions about stability and reward exploitation, and the paper would be stronger with a clearer explanation of why this training setup was reliable in practice.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored setting: multi-page clinical documents, which are significantly harder for LLMs compared to single image or text-only tasks. The pointer-based evidence grounding mechanism, which enforces that all claims are referenced back to a “pointer back” of evidence sources, is a well-motivated and practically meaningful design for clinical settings. The two-stage framework (GRPO followed by SFT) is also sensible and motivated by the ablation studies. The authors provide a comprehensive evaluation suite, including validity and grounding metrics, safety, and clinician preference.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There is a crucial disconnect between quantitative metrics and clinician evaluation. In the clinician rubric (Table 4), the Stage2-only model matches or slightly outperforms the full method across multiple dimensions (clinical quality, usability, and overall impression), despite the full method achieving substantially better grounding and diagnostic metrics. This discrepancy is not adequately analyzed. Given the importance of clinician judgment in this domain, it raises questions about whether the proposed improvements on the quantitative metrics translate to meaningful gains in real-world clinical utility. Relatedly, the paper does not clearly discuss the tradeoff between auditability and usability. The pointer-based constraints and evidence budgeting likely make outputs more conservative or rigid, which may improve verifiability but reduce perceived usefulness or fluency. While the pointer mechanism is novel and compelling, the overall modeling approach is still somewhat incremental, relying on a combination of GRPO and SFT. The novelty lies more in the problem formulation and constraints than in fundamentally new techniques. Additionally, the dataset is relatively small (657 studies) and drawn from a single center, which raises some concerns about generalization. There is no external validation or cross-institution evaluation. Some design choices, like the fixed evidence atom budget of K=6, why some information like the treatment label are left unpointerized, and sensitivity of the results to the specific constraints or reward design, are not fully justified. Further, a published codebase would help support reproducibility.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper tackles a real clinical-document problem that is more realistic than standard medical VQA. Multi-page PSG reports with mixed plots, indices, and narrative context are genuinely difficult inputs for current multimodal models. 2.The pointer-grounded output representation is directionally sensible. Restricting evidence citations to a controlled pointer space is a practical way to improve auditability relative to unconstrained justification text. 3.The paper evaluates more than just task accuracy. It includes parseability, pointer validity, over-diagnosis under indeterminate evidence, and a clinician-facing rubric, which is better than reporting one headline metric. 4.The ablation that removes Stage 1 does show that the alignment stage improves parsing and grounding under the authors’ setup, so the two-stage design is not entirely vacuous.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The empirical validation is much weaker than the presentation suggests. The dataset has 657 instances but only 136 patients from a single tertiary center, and the test set is just 100 instances. For a clinically heterogeneous sleep-diagnosis task, this is a very small basis for broad claims about reliable structured clinical decision support. 2.The key claim that the full method is better is not consistently supported by the authors’ own results. In Table 3, the ablation without the Pointer Bank actually has higher insomnia subtype F1 than the full method, and in Table 4 the Stage2-only model has the best aggregate clinician scores. This directly undermines the implied narrative that the full TRACE-PSG stack is clearly superior overall. 3.The paper overclaims on safety and hallucination. All three models receive 0.0 percent critical error and 0.0 percent hallucination in the 100-case clinician review, and all three have 0 percent safety violation in the rule-based evaluation. When even weaker ablations look equally perfect on safety, the metric is probably not sensitive enough, the rubric is too coarse, or the task has been defined too conservatively. In any case, these numbers are not persuasive evidence of real clinical safety. 4.The method’s novelty is limited. Pointer-restricted evidence citation, schema-constrained generation, warm-starting from extraction alignment, and reward-based extraction tuning are all recognizable ingredients rather than a fundamentally new MICCAI-level method. The paper packages them cleanly for PSG reports, but the algorithmic advance itself is modest. 5.The paper’s auditability story is incomplete. Diagnosis and notes are pointerized, but treatment is intentionally left unpointerized free-form text. That is exactly the portion where clinically harmful recommendations would matter most. As a result, the system is only partially auditable, while the title and framing suggest broader traceability than the implementation actually delivers.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers and meta-reviewer for their comments. [Meta/R2: limited baselines; Pointer Bank/budget may favor verifiability metrics] We agree these gains indicate controllability/auditability, not broad clinical-reasoning superiority. Our comparisons ask whether scale/instruction following suffices for auditable PSG diagnosis and whether report-reading alignment improves grounding/abstention. Qwen3-VL-8B has high Grounding Pass but lower Pointer F1 and insomnia F1, showing format compliance does not ensure correct evidence/diagnosis. We will clarify in Sec. 4.[R3/R4: TRACE-PSG combines known components, not a new architecture] It is not a generic architecture contribution but a PSG-specific auditable formulation integrating report reading, pointerized provenance, bounded evidence, and abstention-aware evaluation. We will revise the contribution statement. [Meta/R2/R3/R4: full model improves automatic metrics but not clinician aggregates; ablations are slightly higher on some scores] TRACE-PSG is not claimed to dominate every metric. Its advantage is auditable/controllable structured support, measured by parseability, pointer grounding, evidence bounding, and abstention: Stage2-only shows 13.95% OSA OverDx, while TRACE-PSG reduces this to 0%. Clinician aggregates include less-atomized treatment/readability/usability aspects; the small Table 4 differences suggest these auditability gains do not cost clinician-facing quality. Thus, Table 4 marks the system boundary rather than contradicting the main claim. We will make this explicit. [R3: pointer constraints may reduce usability] The clinician rubric shows no usability/readability collapse; scores remain high. With improved pointer validity/grounding, this suggests better auditability without clear usability loss. We will clarify this. [R4: treatment is unpointerized despite the auditability framing] TRACE-PSG provides field-level auditability for diagnosis/evidence/notes, not every generated word or treatment recommendation. We will state pointer-grounded treatment as future work. [Meta/R3/R4: single-center small cohort/no external validation; R2: generalization concern] We agree the 657-study/136-patient single-center cohort with 100 test cases does not establish deployment/external reliability. We will temper the claim: the evidence supports retrospective internal feasibility of an auditable PSG formulation, not external validation of a deployable system. Physician-derived labels and patient-level splitting prevent multi-night leakage. [R2: insomnia-dominant data and site-specific conventions may limit portability] We agree this limits external generalization. TRACE-PSG uses predefined metric/note pointers and structured labels, making evidence explicit and auditable, but portability across templates still requires multi-center validation. We will state this. [R4: 0% safety/critical-error/hallucination rates do not prove real-world safety] These zero rates are minimum safety screens, not the sole safety evidence. More discriminative is abstention: Stage2-only has 13.95% OSA OverDx under indeterminate evidence, while TRACE-PSG reduces it to 0%, suggesting fewer unsafe forced diagnoses. We will distinguish limited checks from deployment-level safety validation. [R2: beta=0 may affect GRPO stability/reward exploitation] Stage 1 is constrained metric extraction with format-gated rule rewards, short training, and parsing/extraction monitoring, reducing reward-exploitation risk. We will clarify this. [R3: K=6 and reward/constraint sensitivity need justification] K=6 forces a small set of key, non-redundant evidence atoms clinicians can audit efficiently, rather than long exhaustive rationales. We will clarify this and discuss sensitivity to budget/reward design. [R3/R4: reproducibility and ethics details are insufficient] Data are de-identified; public release may be privacy-restricted. We will provide details and release code/prompts where permitted.

title: TrustSyn: Reliable and Divergent Synergy for Mixed-Domain Fundus Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Mixed-domain semi-supervised fundus segmentation is an important yet challenging scenario, as it combines label scarcity with domain shift across centers and devices. The problem is well motivated from both the methodological and application perspectives. 2.Integrating MedSAM with U-Net is a reasonable and practically relevant design. The paper does not treat the foundation model merely as a stronger teacher, but attempts to combine its robust global priors with the conventional model’s adaptability to domain-specific details, which is an appealing perspective. 3.The proposed SRA mechanism goes beyond image-level confidence by estimating reliability at the local spatial level, which is particularly relevant for fundus structures with ambiguous cup-disc boundaries. This fine-grained treatment is interesting because it allows supervision to adapt to local uncertainty instead of relying on a single global criterion.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.In the current design, the spatial reliability map is constructed from the agreement between the student U-Net and teacher U-Net, as well as between the teacher U-Net and teacher MedSAM. While this is intuitive, local agreement does not always imply local correctness, especially in low-contrast or ambiguous cup-disc boundary regions where multiple branches may share similar biases. Moreover, the reliability estimation already depends in part on the current student state, which may introduce a degree of circularity in pseudo-label selection. 2.The paper motivates FD as a way to encourage feature orthogonality and prevent representational collapse. However, the implemented loss minimizes cosine similarity between projected features, which more directly pushes the two branches toward opposite directions rather than strict orthogonality. The paper argues that the primary segmentation objective balances this effect in practice, but this mechanism would benefit from clearer explanation or stronger empirical validation. 3.The framework involves multiple important settings, including the sliding-window configuration and overlap ratio in SRA, the Hanning weighting, the parameters in uncertainty weighting, the confidence threshold for reliable regions, and the balancing coefficients in the total objective. Since these choices affect pseudo-label generation, supervision strength, and feature regularization simultaneously, more systematic sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence in the method’s robustness.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a mixed-domain semi-supervised method to address coarse-grained reliability estimation and representational collapse, which offers a certain degree of novelty. 2.The comparison and ablation studies on fundus image segmentation support its effectiveness. 3.The paper is well organized and logically clear.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.In the proposed SRA, what are the differences between Self-Confidence and Mutual-Confidence and the Self-Confidence and Mutual-Confidence introduced in Steady Progress Beats Stagnation: Mutual Aid of Foundation and Conventional Models in Mixed Domain Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation? I do not see a proper citation or a clear discussion of what is adopted and what is different. If this work introduces improvements, the paper should provide evidence that these improvements are effective. Although the current ablation includes an analysis of SPA, it is still unclear whether the performance gain comes from the original Self-Confidence and Mutual-Confidence in SynFoC or from the proposed modifications. 2.What does $\lambda_h$ in Eq.~(5) denote? This symbol is not defined. 3.In Table~1, although TrustSyn achieves better results on Domains 1 and 4, its performance is much worse than that of existing state-of-the-art methods on Domains 2 and 3, especially on Domain 2.An analysis of these failure cases is important for understanding the boundary of the proposed method. 4.In Table~2, some components bring only marginal improvements. It is unclear whether these small gains are statistically meaningful or simply due to randomness. 5.The ablation study lacks an analysis of sensitivity to key hyperparameters.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) The problem addressed is novel, and the identification of representation collapse in the collaborative framework between foundation models and conventional models is insightful and inspiring. (2) The model architecture is logically clear and well structured, representing a strong extension and improvement over popular methods in this field. (3) The method achieves strong experimental performance. The ablation studies are comprehensive, and the progressive integration of different modules yields consistent performance gains.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) The proposed method introduces two lightweight modules on top of the foundation-model-based teacher–student collaborative framework. While the network design is reasonable, the level of novelty is somewhat limited. Using Shannon entropy to generate uncertainty maps and modulate supervision signals is a common practice in semi-supervised learning, and the FD module largely reuses the cosine-similarity minimization strategy from [25]. (2) The term 𝜆 in Equation 5 is not explained in the paper. (3) Based on the statistical orthogonality observed during cosine-similarity minimization, the paper directly claims that the latent representations are kept orthogonal. This statement is not mathematically rigorous enough.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and Reviewers for the comments. 1.Novelty & Relation to Prior Work (R3, R4) SRA vs. SynFoC (R3): SRA upgrades SynFoC from coarse image-level confidence to fine-grained spatial confidence. 1) Methodological difference: Unlike SynFoC’s scalar confidence, SRA constructs spatial reliability maps via sliding windows and Hanning weighting, capturing boundary heterogeneity. 2) Empirical net gain: In Tab. 2, “Base” is original SynFoC. “Base+SRA” replaces its image-level confidence with our spatial confidence. This replacement yields a consistent performance improvement, representing the net gain of our adaptation. Tab. 1 shows TrustSyn outperforms the full SynFoC baseline on average. We will add proper citations. FD & UW (R4): We uniquely adapt established math to integrate Foundation Models (FMs) with conventional models. 1) Heterogeneous regularization (FD): Unlike [25], which minimizes cosine-similarity to prevent homogeneous CNN collapse globally, TrustSyn addresses representational collapse between highly heterogeneous architectures (MedSAM and U-Net) by selectively applying FD within our dynamically estimated reliable regions. 2) Differentiable soft-gating (UW): Instead of binary thresholding, we leverage the FM’s zero-shot entropy for a differentiable soft-gating mechanism, preventing abrupt supervision loss in ambiguous zones under severe domain shifts. 2.Math Rigor & Terminology (R2, R4) R2 and R4 correctly note our FD loss (minimizing 1+cos) pushes representations toward opposite directions rather than strict orthogonality. We will refine our terminology to “feature divergence”, clarifying its mechanism through two aspects. 1) Theoretical equilibrium: While L_dis pushes features apart, the primary segmentation objective constrains both branches to maintain semantic coherence. Since strict diametric opposition prevents shared decoding, the system reaches a dynamic equilibrium, a phenomenon also observed in [25]. 2) Empirical validation: Consistent with [25], we will add an empirical analysis of training dynamics, confirming L_dis reliably converges around 1.0 (cos near 0), providing the statistical validation requested by R2.3.Domains 2/3 & Failure Analysis (R3) We acknowledge the Domain 2 performance gap compared to reported SOTA and analyze its causes. 1) Unified setup: Reproducing baselines under a unified codebase introduces natural metric variations, yet TrustSyn remains highly competitive. 2) Failure analysis: Per R3, we analyzed Domain 2 failure cases. In severely degraded images with low contrast and blurry boundaries, TrustSyn acts conservatively: UW suppresses high-entropy signals and FD remains inactive. This limits aggressive adaptation but prevents confirmation bias, yielding the highest overall robustness. We will incorporate this discussion. 4.Hyperparameters & Stats (R2, R3) We verify parameter robustness and statistical significance. 1) Parameter robustness (R2): SRA is insensitive to window/overlap partitions due to Hanning weighting. Coefficients (α, β) are stable across broad ranges. UW’s soft-gating prevents hard thresholding drops, rendering T_c fluctuations negligible (0.80-0.95). 2) Statistical significance (R3): Tab. 2 gains are statistically significant (paired t-test, p < 0.05). Though progressive DSC gains appear modest, the modules synergistically drive substantial reductions in geometric errors, effectively correcting vital boundaries. 5.Notation (R3, R4) λ_h in Eq. 5 scales entropy-based modulation in UW. We will explicitly define this. 6.Circularity (R2) To prevent circularity from shared biases in ambiguous regions: 1) EMA temporally decouples the teacher. 2) FD structurally enforces feature divergence, reaching consensus via distinct pathways. 3) UW down-weights supervision in high-entropy regions, avoiding false agreement memorization. 7.Reproducibility (R4) We commit to open-sourcing the full codebase upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewers consistently recognize the paper’s strengths: a timely and important problem (mixed-domain semi-supervised fundus segmentation), a well-motivated integration of MedSAM and U-Net, and solid ablation studies. While Reviewer #3 gives a Weak Reject, the concerns raised — lack of clarity on differences from prior work (SynFoC), weaker performance on two domains, missing statistical testing, and insufficient hyperparameter sensitivity analysis — are all addressable during rebuttal. Importantly, Reviewer #3 explicitly states that the score may be raised if concerns are adequately addressed. No reviewer identifies a fatal methodological flaw. Therefore, the paper should proceed to the rebuttal phase, with the expectation that the authors provide a thorough response addressing the noted concerns and strengthening the experimental analysis. | The paper does not convincingly distinguish itself from the prior SynFoC framework. The rebuttal’s claim that SynFoC uses only “image level” confidence is inaccurate (SynFoC operates at the pixel level), so the asserted novelty of “spatial” reliability is unfounded. Moreover, the method performs substantially worse than existing SOTA on two of the four test domains, and the rebuttal’s explanation (that the model deliberately suppresses adaptation in difficult cases) actually confirms a lack of robustness. Reviewer #4 also notes that key components largely reuse existing ideas. These core issues cannot be fixed during rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal, all reviewers agreed that the paper should be accepted. The Area Chair supports this consensus and recommends acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two accept and one missing after rebuttal. I agree and would accept the paper.

title: TSegAgent: Zero-Shot Tooth Segmentation via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Agents
reviewer_1_strengths: The major strength of this paper is its fundamental shift in how tooth segmentation and identification are approached, moving away from conventional supervised learning toward a reasoning-driven, zero-shot paradigm. Rather than training task-specific models on large annotated datasets, the authors reformulate the problem as one of structured geometric reasoning, where predictions are inferred through a combination of visual evidence and explicit anatomical constraints. This reframing is both novel and significant, as it directly addresses the high annotation cost and limited generalization that characterize existing dental AI methods. Building on this formulation, the paper introduces a geometry-aware vision-language agent that performs tooth identification through a sequence of interpretable, multi-stage reasoning steps. Instead of relying on a single-pass prediction, the method decomposes the task into sub-problems such as non-tooth filtering, central incisor identification, and full-arch classification, followed by an explicit error detection and correction mechanism.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Lack of transparency in prompt design and reproducibility concerns. The proposed framework relies heavily on vision-language prompting and multi-round conversational reasoning, yet the paper does not provide sufficient details of the prompts used in the experiments. While the authors mention that “detailed prompt design can be found in the source code”, the absence of prompt specifications in the paper itself limits reproducibility and scientific scrutiny. Given that prompt engineering is a core component of the method, this omission prevents readers from: (a) Understanding how geometric priors are operationalized in the VLM. (b) Assessing robustness to prompt variations. (c) Reproducing or extending the approach without relying on external resources. 2.Dependence on a single proprietary VLM without comparative analysis. The method is evaluated using a single vision-language model (“ChatGPT 5.2”), which introduces several concerns: (a) Lack of ablation across VLMs: It is unclear whether the performance gains are due to the proposed framework or the specific capabilities of this particular model. (b) Limited generalizability: The method’s effectiveness with other VLMs (e. g. , open-source or smaller models) is not demonstrated. (c) Reproducibility and accessibility issues: The reliance on a proprietary, potentially costly API raises barriers for adoption and independent validation. A more complete study would include comparisons across multiple VLMs (e. g. , GPT-4V-like systems, open-source multimodal models) or at least a sensitivity analysis. 3.Use of non-standard metrics without sufficient explanation. The paper reports evaluation metrics such as TLA, TSA, and TIR, but does not clearly define their full forms or provide sufficient intuition regarding their interpretation. (a) These metrics are not standard in segmentation literature, and their clinical or methodological significance is not adequately explained. (b) The paper introduces abbreviations (e. g. , TLA, TSA, TIR, GT) without consistently defining them upon first use. (c) Readers unfamiliar with the Teeth3DS benchmark may find it difficult to assess the practical relevance of the reported improvements. 4.Unclear reporting of variability (± values). Performance metrics are reported with mean ± values, but the paper does not explicitly state: (a) What these values represent (standard deviation, standard error, or confidence intervals). (b) How they computed. Without this clarification, it is difficult to assess the stability of the approach and whether improvements over baselines are meaningful. 5.Absence of statistical significance analysis. Although the paper reports quantitative improvements over prior methods (Table 1, page 8), it does not include any statistical significance testing (e. g. , p-values, confidence intervals). Given that some improvements appear incremental, the lack of statistical analysis makes it unclear whether: (a) The observed gains are statistically significant. (b) The method consistently outperforms baselines across samples. This is particularly important in medical imaging, where rigorous validation standards are expected. 6.Limited transparency and characterization of the private dataset. The paper evaluates generalization on a private dataset (340 scans), but provides insufficient details regarding: (a) Data distribution (scanner types, patient demographics, pathology diversity) (b) Differences relative to Teeth3DS (domain shift characterization) (c) Annotation protocol and quality control Furthermore, the dataset is not publicly available, limiting reproducibility. There is no quantitative analysis of how domain shift affects performance. While the inclusion of external validation is a strength, the lack of transparency reduces its impact. 7.Methodological clarity and completeness of description. While the overall pipeline is conceptually clear (Fig. 1, page 3), several components lack sufficient technical detail: (a) The mask merging strategy across views is described heuristically but lacks formalization or algorithmic clarity. (b) The interaction between geometric priors and VLM reasoning is not rigorously specified. (c) The error correction mechanism is described at a high level without precise implementation details. As a result, it may be difficult for readers to fully understand how the system behaves in edge cases and reproduce the pipeline without access to code. 8.Lack of clear architectural specification of the proposed framework. Although the paper presents an overall pipeline (e. g. , Fig. 1, page 3), it lacks a precise and formal description of the framework architecture. The interactions between components—such as SAM3-based segmentation, geometric processing, and the vision-language reasoning agent—are described at a high level but not specified in a rigorous or modular manner. In particular: (a) The data flow between modules is not formally defined. (b) The interfaces between geometric priors and VLM reasoning remain implicit. (c) The multi-round conversational process is not represented as a structured algorithm or state machine As a result, it is difficult to reconstruct the full pipeline without relying on external code, understand how different components contribute quantitatively to the final output, and compare the framework with existing architectures in a systematic way. A clearer architectural description (e. g. , formal pipeline diagram, pseudo-code, or modular breakdown) would significantly improve clarity, reproducibility, and scientific rigor.

author_feedback: [R1.1,R3.1,R3.5 Prompt] The prompt consists of both textual instructions and annotated images. In images, tooth masks are colored with labeled text, indicating each instance. We ask the VLM to first identify non-tooth masks, then determine the central-incisor IDs to separate the left and right sides, and finally classify each instance’s tooth type based on its shape and anatomical position. We take into account the characteristics of dental data, including the dental arch order to guide tooth arrangement and tooth volume information to help the VLM distinguish and order individual teeth. Their effectiveness has been validated through our ablation studies. Without geometric priors, the VLM is more prone to errors in FDI ordering and instance-ID recognition. [R1.2,R2.1 VLM reliance] Preliminary trials with other VLMs (like open sourced GLM-5 and Doubao seed 2.0) remained competitive to other baselines, but ChatGPT gave the best result. However, the focus is the zero-shot geometry-aware reasoning framework rather than optimizing the choice of VLM. [R1.3,R3.4 Metrics] TLA is mean of normalized Euclidean distance between GT teeth centroids and the closest localized teeth centroid. TSA is the average F1-score over all instances. TIR is the percentage of true identification cases relative to all GT teeth in the testing set. Their formulas are defined within the paper. These metrics are appropriate for this task because they separately evaluate localization, segmentation, and identification, while mIoU provides an additional standard overlap-based reference. [R1.4,R1.5 Statistics] We use mean standard deviation across test scans, which is a common convention in machine learning. We’ll clarify that. Regarding statistical significance, we agree that p-values or confidence intervals could provide an additional statistical perspective, but current results indicate not only higher average performance but also stronger stability under domain shift. Therefore, while formal significance testing could further strengthen the statistical analysis, the reported values already support the robustness trend observed in our experiments. [R1.6,R2.2 Private dataset] The private dataset follows the same annotation scheme as Teeth3DS produced by experienced dentists. The data were obtained by scanning plaster dental models using a desktop scanner, and include diverse challenging cases such as missing teeth, crowding, bubbles in models, defects, and other dental abnormalities. We can make the data publicly available. We disagree that the evaluation inherently favors TSegAgent, the goal of this experiment is to evaluate zero-shot cross-domain transfer without target-domain annotations, while domain adaptation or fine-tuning baselines would require labeled target-domain data and therefore correspond to a different setting. The domain shift is quantitatively reflected by the clear degradation of supervised baselines on the private dataset, whereas TSegAgent maintains stronger performance and stability. [R1.7,R1.8 Details] We have clearly described the entire framework in an algorithmic and formulaic manner through Fig. 1 and Sec. 2.The geometric priors help reorder masks and are filled in text prompts, which can be found in the code. [R1.7,R3.2,R3.3 Error correction] The module only identifies and corrects wrong FDI predictions, not segmentation masks. The dental arch can imply symmetry and ordering of teeth ID, through this feature, we can propose potential errors to VLM, and let VLM reconsider its prediction to the right one. Segmentation improvements mainly come from non-tooth filtering and over-segmentation removal, while error correction mainly improves FDI accuracy. [R2.3 Cost] In thinking mode, each case costs 6284 tokens and around 120 seconds on average, which is acceptable for offline analysis and much faster than manual annotation. It would be more economical and faster without thinking mode, however, performance may be slightly reduced.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces TSegAgent, a zero-shot tooth segmentation framework that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as reasoning agents to provide anatomical guidance for downstream segmentation models. The core idea is genuinely novel: rather than training task-specific segmentation networks, the authors propose using a ChatGPT 5.2 VLM to reason about dental anatomy, generate geometric priors, and direct a foundation segmentation model (e.g., SAM) to produce tooth delineations without any fine-tuning on target data. The reported cross-domain generalization results—are indeed promising and address a critical clinical bottleneck, namely the prohibitive cost of manual annotation across diverse imaging modalities. However, the paper suffers from two fundamental weaknesses that the reviewers correctly identified. First, there is a Reproducibility Crisis: the entire pipeline depends on a proprietary, closed-source VLM (ChatGPT 5.2), which is not publicly accessible, version-controlled, or reproducible by the community. As R1 and R3 both noted (scores of 3), this dependency makes it impossible for other researchers to verify, replicate, or build upon the work. The authors provide no fallback using open-source alternatives (e.g., LLaVA, GPT-4V, or other openly available VLMs), nor do they specify the exact prompting strategy with sufficient detail to allow approximate reproduction. This is a serious methodological concern for a MICCAI publication. Second, there is an Evaluation Rigor issue. The paper introduces three non-standard metrics—Tooth Localization Accuracy (TLA), Tooth Segmentation Accuracy (TSA), and Tooth Identification Rate (TIR)—without providing clear formal definitions, mathematical formulations, or references to established evaluation protocols. As R2 (score of 4) pointed out, while the approach is intriguing, the lack of standard metrics (e.g., Dice, IoU, Hausdorff distance) makes it difficult to compare against existing benchmarks or to assess clinical significance. R3 further highlighted that the ablation studies are insufficient, and the reported improvements lack statistical significance testing. Despite these limitations, the paper’s novelty and potential clinical impact are high. The idea of using VLMs for anatomical reasoning as a zero-shot segmentation strategy represents a paradigm shift that could significantly reduce annotation burden in medical imaging. The reviews collectively suggest that the core contribution is valuable but requires substantial strengthening in reproducibility and evaluation rigor. | Two reviewers support acceptance (R2=4, R3=3→Accept). Rebuttal effectively addressed VLM dependency concerns (shown to be ~6284 tokens, ~120s/case), runtime cost, and private dataset fairness. Zero-shot tooth segmentation is a clinically relevant problem with promising cross-domain generalization. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers agreed the core idea is novel and the cross-domain results are strong and clinically relevant. The rebuttal addressed the main concerns well. Two reviewers found the rebuttal convincing, with only a minor camera-ready clarification (how SAM3 masks are refined) outstanding. The novelty and practical relevance outweigh the remaining gaps, and I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This is a borderline paper with mixed reviews. While reviewers agreed that the paper introduces a novel, reasoning-driven zero-shot paradigm for tooth segmentation and identification, and that it demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization without requiring large annotated datasets, they also raised serious concerns about the paper’s soundness and reproducibility: (1)​the heavy reliance on a proprietary, closed-source VLM limits scientific rigor and makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of the proposed geometric reasoning framework from the raw power of the model; (2)​key methodological details—such as prompt design, architectural specifications, and the segmentation refinement mechanism—are insufficiently transparent, hindering reproducibility; and (3)​the evaluation lacks statistical analysis and uses non-standard metrics without adequate explanation, while the private dataset comparison may unfairly favor the zero-shot approach. The rebuttal provided clarifications on runtime, dataset characteristics, and preliminary tests with open-source VLMs, which partially addressed these concerns. After careful deliberation, I recommend accepting this manuscript due to its technical novelty.

title: Unlocking the Power of Medical Tabular Data via Semantic-Aware Multimodal Pre-training
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Clinically grounded problem formulation. The two-dimensional hierarchical structure hypothesis (inter-feature importance and intra-feature continuity-discreteness duality) is not an abstract theoretical construct but directly reflects how clinicians reason about structured patient data. This conceptual framing is the paper’s most original contribution and provides a coherent motivation for both proposed modules. 2.Strong out-of-domain generalization. The geographically isolated OOD test set on SLICE-3D is a rigorous evaluation design rarely seen in multimodal pre-training papers. Achieving an OOD AUC of 0.944 versus 0.911 for the strongest baseline (TIP) is a substantial and clinically meaningful margin. Furthermore, the linear probe AUC of 0.984 surpassing TIP’s full fine-tuning AUC of 0.971 demonstrates exceptional representation quality. 3.Thorough and honest ablation study. Table 2 systematically evaluates not only the presence or absence of each module, but also compares multiple alternative design choices for discretization (equal-width bins, hard-label quantile, Gaussian kernel, triangle kernel). The finding that the simpler triangle kernel outperforms the heavier Gaussian kernel is a practically useful and honestly reported result. 4.Label-free importance estimation is well-designed. Using PCA pseudo-labels to drive a frozen TabPFN v2 meta-prior for feature importance extraction is a principled approach that avoids label leakage while capturing dataset-specific feature interactions. This design choice reflects careful thinking about the practical constraints of medical pre-training. 5.Cross-specialty validation strengthens generalizability claims. Applying the framework to EyePACS (ophthalmology) in addition to dermatology datasets provides meaningful evidence that the two-dimensional structural hypothesis holds across medical domains, not just within the training specialty. 6.Qualitative analysis corroborates quantitative gains. The t-SNE visualizations and attention heatmaps in Figure 3 provide interpretable evidence that the soft-label objective produces semantically organized latent clusters and clinically meaningful attention distributions, supporting the mechanistic claims of the paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Sensitivity to the number of discretization bins (B) is not evaluated. The framework uses B=50 quantile bins, but this hyperparameter directly controls the granularity of the soft-label distributions and the smoothness of ordinal preservation. No ablation study is provided for B, and it is unclear whether performance is robust to this choice across datasets with different feature distributions. A brief sensitivity analysis in the supplementary would address this concern. 2.Computational cost of the importance estimation step is not reported. The paper states that TabPFN v2 feature importance extraction is performed strictly offline prior to pre-training, but does not report the wall-clock time or memory requirements for this step. For practitioners working with large-scale datasets (e. g. , SLICE-3D with 400,000 images), this information is relevant for assessing the practical overhead of adopting the framework. 3.The three-head ensemble mechanism is insufficiently described. Section 3.1 mentions that downstream evaluation uses a “three-head ensemble mechanism that averages distinct classification logits,” but does not specify what the three heads are or how they differ. No ablation is provided to justify this design choice over a single-head classifier. 4.The high maximum masking rate may raise stability concerns. With rbase=0.1 and alpha=rmax=0.7, the most important features can receive a masking rate of up to 0.8.While the paper reports stable training, no analysis or discussion is provided regarding potential optimization instability at this extreme masking rate, particularly for datasets with fewer training samples. 5.The HOP private dataset limits full reproducibility. HOP is a private institutional dataset and no detailed statistics (class distribution, image acquisition protocol, patient demographics) are provided. reviewer_2_strengths: Critical analysis: The authors provide a precise critique of the TIP architecture’s limitations, followed by a well-justified technical framework designed specifically to address those gaps. Methodological soundness: Leveraging TabPFN v2 for feature importance is a sophisticated choice, as it effectively incorporates the specific inductive biases required for tabular data into the pre-training phase. Comprehensive benchmarking: The evaluation is thorough, providing a detailed comparison against both state-of-the-art methods and established baselines across multiple datasets. Exhaustive ablation studies: The ablation experiments are particularly rigorous; by testing alternative discretization methods and kernels, the authors provide strong empirical justification for selecting the triangle kernel. Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is highly organized and technically detailed, supported by clear visualizations that make the complex multimodal architecture accessible.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The methodological novelty appears incremental relative to the TIP architecture. To better showcase the significance of these enhancements, the authors should consolidate their results by including robust statistical reporting, such as standard deviations, confidence intervals, or p-values. Given that a 5-fold cross-validation was conducted, providing these metrics is essential to confirm that the observed 2%–4% gains are statistically significant and not due to stochastic variation. Methodological clarifications: Aggregation formalism: Section 2.2 describes extracting importance from query, key, and self-attention matrices across 12 layers but lacks a formal definition of the “aggregation” process. The authors should provide the mathematical notation detailing how multi-head, multi-layer attention weights are collapsed into a final importance score (e.g., via Attention Rollout, simple averaging, or a specific weighted heuristic). Sample heterogeneity: Since TabPFN generates sample-specific attention maps, the authors should clarify how inter-row variability is managed. If the importance scores are averaged into a global metric, a justification is needed for bypassing inter-sample heterogeneity, which is often a critical factor in diverse medical cohorts. Loss formulation: The notation in Equation 2 is somewhat ambiguous; specifically, using “CE” and “KL” for a single sample-category item is misleading. A more rigorous formulation of the Discretized Reconstruction loss is required to improve technical clarity. Suggestions for strengthening the contribution: Foundation model integration: While TabPFN v2 is utilized for feature importance extraction, the authors might consider whether using it directly as a backbone feature extractor—providing embeddings as model inputs in addition to masking weights—could further enhance performance. Minor improvements: Visual consistency: If the feature importance is a primary driver for the masking mechanism, this should be explicitly illustrated or mentioned in the second diagram of Figure 1, where the masking process is currently omitted.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for appreciating AID’s clinical importance and methodological grounding. The central contribution is a semantic-aware pre-training formulation that treats structured clinical variables as supervision signals for image-tabular medical representation learning. We address concerns below. Q1: Novelty beyond TIP and relation to TP-BERTa (R2, R3). In contrast to TIP/MMCL/CITab’s semantic-agnostic flat-vector treatment with uniform masking and continuous regression, AID models inter-feature diagnostic hierarchy via a label-free importance curriculum and intra-feature ordinal-continuous structure via soft-label discretized reconstruction. We thank R3 for pointing to TP-BERTa, whose goal is orthogonal: it encodes ordinality at the input-tokenization level for a unimodal tabular LM, while AID enforces it at the reconstruction-objective level inside image-tabular multimodal pre-training, where visual evidence reconstructs masked clinical semantics. Empirically (Tab.1), AID’s linear probing exceeds prior SSL baselines’ full fine-tuning (incl. TIP, 0.984 vs 0.971), with OOD 0.944 vs 0.911 showing gains from semantic-aware design, not scaling. TP-BERTa will be cited and contrasted in camera-ready. Q2: TabPFN role, aggregation, masking stability (R1, R2, R3). TabPFN serves only as an offline label-free meta-prior for dataset-level feature hierarchy. Designed for small-scale tabular data, it is applied once offline rather than as a backbone for 400K cohorts. For aggregation (R2), each layer averages multi-head weights; feature saliency from query (row sum, outgoing influence), key (column sum, incoming relevance) and self-attention (diagonal, self-relevance) is summed across layers, L1-normalized and min-max scaled, yielding a closed-form heuristic, not Attention Rollout. Formal notation will be added to §2.2.For row heterogeneity (R2), TabPFN’s in-context inference uses a single PCA-pseudo-label across rows, producing a dataset-level vector by construction. By design, it serves as a cohort-level masking prior, not a patient-specific explanation; patient-level heterogeneity is modeled by the multimodal encoder during representation learning. We clarify that s_i is fixed by design as the label-free curriculum; the representation evolves under it (Fig.3(e,f)). The per-feature cap α=r_max=0.7 (R1) applies only to top-importance features; the dataset-level expected ratio stays ~0.3, so adaptive masking targets clinically salient features rather than masking more. On joint training (R3), a jointly trained visual prior captures image-token saliency from multimodal optimization, whereas TabPFN supplies a tabular bias before pre-training (future work). Q3: Soft-label discretized reconstruction (R1, R3). On bin sensitivity (R1), B∈{20,50,100} shows an inverted-U with B=50 consistently best (smaller B over-smooths intervals; larger B approaches noisy regression). Unlike hard quantile discretization, the triangle-kernel preserves ordinal neighborhood structure; unlike Gaussian smoothing it avoids over-smoothing while distinguishing near-bin from far-bin errors. The DR loss notation in Eq.2 will be refined to clarify summation over samples, features and bins (R2). Q4: Statistical reliability and three-head protocol (R1, R2). Due to space, fold-wise std was omitted; in our 5-fold protocol AID’s std (≈0.5%) stays below TIP’s (≈1%), placing the OOD margin well outside fold-to-fold variation. The three-head ensemble averages image-only, tabular-only and multimodal logits, applied uniformly to AID and baselines (per TIP/CITab), giving no AID-specific advantage; representation quality is evidenced by linear probing surpassing prior baselines’ full fine-tuning. Minor. DINOv3 is self-supervised in pre-training but grouped with supervised methods because we fine-tuned its weights with labels; we will relabel it as “SSL”. More implementation details and full results will be made publicly available.

title: WaveDE: Wavelet-Routed Dual-Expert Network for Fundus Photograph Enhancement
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Large-scale experiments and comprehensive evaluation framework. 2) Explicitly decomposing composite degradations into low-frequency global degradations and high-frequency local artifacts has a solid signal processing foundation. The structural guidance map G introduces meaningful interaction between experts rather than independent processing.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Training relies entirely on programmatically synthesized degradations (brightness, contrast, saturation, halo, dark spots, noise, blur, and combinations). However, real clinical degradations are more complex (e. g. , optical aberrations, cataracts, vitreous opacity, tear film instability). Although the paper acknowledges this gap, it provides limited validation on real unpaired low-quality images (only MR-ART). Downstream evaluations (Table 2) still rely on synthetic degradations, failing to demonstrate effectiveness on real data. This is a critical limitation for clinical translation. 2.WaveDE combines SD v1.5 U-Net, FD-Block (VMamba + asymmetric convolutions), HFI-VAE decoder, and two teacher networks (U-Net++, PraNet). However, the paper does not report model size, training time, inference latency, or GPU memory usage. Training is conducted on RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), which exceeds typical clinical deployment conditions. Efficiency analysis is essential for practical applicability. 3.The structural guidance map (G) is claimed to enable meaningful interaction between experts. However, ablation only evaluates the presence/absence of FD-Block as a whole, without isolating the contribution of (G). A variant without guidance would strengthen this claim. 4.VMamba is used for long-range modeling, but no comparison is provided with alternatives such as Transformers or CNNs. The choice appears driven by complexity rather than task-specific necessity. 5.Datasets such as RFMiD and FIVES are included in both training and downstream evaluation. Although training uses synthetic pairs, exposure to high-quality images may bias results. This issue is not discussed. 6.The use of PraNet for optic disc detection lacks justification. Fixed weights ((\lambda_v), (\lambda_{od})) and spatial coefficients (Eq. 7) are not analyzed.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: In real-world fundus image acquisition, multiple degradations often co-occur, whereas many existing methods are still designed around single-degradation settings. Therefore, the two core challenges identified by the authors, namely compound degradations and the conflict between global correction and fine-detail recovery, are well motivated. The problem formulation is clear, the application background is realistic, and the overall motivation is sound. The proposed method is built around the central idea of frequency decoupling. DWT is used to separate frequency bands, which are then processed by dedicated low- and high-frequency experts. The high-frequency-injected VAE decoder and anatomical regularization further strengthen detail recovery and structural fidelity. The authors report not only PSNR and SSIM for image restoration, but also evaluate the effect of the enhanced images on downstream classification and segmentation tasks, and further include OOD evaluation on PAPILA and ARIA. This goes beyond showing that the images merely “look better” and attempts to demonstrate that the enhancement is beneficial for downstream medical image analysis. In particular, in Table 1, the proposed method achieves clearly better PSNR and SSIM than the compared methods on both the full test set and the different subsets, indicating strong overall performance. The emphasis on anatomical consistency is also well aligned with the requirements of medical imaging tasks. Rather than focusing only on visual quality, the authors additionally use vessel and optic disc priors to constrain the enhancement results, which can help reduce structural artefacts and hallucinated content to some extent. This is meaningful in the medical imaging context.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the improvements in classification and segmentation are a strength of the paper, the main text does not provide sufficiently detailed descriptions of the downstream models, including their specific architectures, training procedures, and whether exactly the same training and evaluation protocol is used for all enhancement methods. Since the downstream results are an important part of the paper’s empirical support, insufficient detail here weakens both the persuasiveness and the reproducibility of the work. The selection of baselines and the fairness of the comparisons could also be improved. In addition to fundus enhancement methods, the paper includes methods originating from other tasks such as super-resolution, image inpainting, and ultrasound imaging. However, not all of these baselines are necessarily the most appropriate or strongest competitors for the specific problem studied here. A comparison more focused on directly relevant fundus or medical image enhancement methods would make the conclusions more convincing. One of the central assumptions of the paper is that different degradations mainly reside in different frequency bands, and can therefore be disentangled through deterministic frequency-band routing. This intuition is reasonable, but at present it is supported mainly indirectly through overall performance and ablation results. The paper lacks more direct analysis showing what the low-frequency and high-frequency experts actually learn, and which types of degradations benefit most from this design.
