author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the problem as “important” (R3), the application background as “realistic” (R2), our “coherent” (R3) and “targeted” (R2) design, the “comprehensive” (R1) and “broad” (R3) evaluation, and the “consistently strong” (R2) performance. Key details below will be added in the camera-ready. 1.R1-W1: Synthetic data. Since paired real LQ–HQ samples are scarce, we generate synthetic data via [23]. It is widely adopted in fundus enhancement, including recent SOTA models MDA [5] and GFE [16]. [23] is physically grounded, explicitly modelling the ophthalmoscope imaging system and real degradation factors. Our synthesis thus approaches the real degradations induced by cataract haze (e.g., brightness/contrast/halo) and vitreous opacity (dark hole + blur). Real paired data are future work. 2.R1-W2: Efficiency & reproducibility. Training and deployment costs differ: 96 GB is for training only; deployment uses ~10 GB on a 24 GB RTX 4090, ~100 ms per image. This is because WaveDE needs only one forward pass (Sec. 2), not iterative diffusion, and the two teachers are dropped at inference (Sec. 2.3). Training details: Sec. 3.1.3.R1-W3: Ablation of G. We agree this would help. The closest existing evidence is w/o FD in Tab. 1 (which removes G together with FD-Block), giving ~2 dB PSNR drops across all subsets. A w/o G ablation is left for future work. 4.R1-W4: VMamba choice. VMamba is task-specific. The LF expert’s global corrections need long-range modelling with preserved spatial structure. CNNs lack long-range capacity; Transformers have weak inductive bias for local structure; VMamba’s 2D selective scan provides both, fitting the task. 5.R1-W5, R3-W1, R3-W3: Data leakage & HQ-exposure bias. Two measures: (i) strictly disjoint splits with no overlap between any training stage (enhancement, ACR teachers, downstream evaluators) and any test split; (ii) WaveDE still ranks first on OOD sets whose HQ images were unseen in training, indicating no HQ-exposure bias. The OD teacher uses Chákṣu/SMDG from the enhancement training split only; the vessel teacher uses DRIVE, LES-AV, TREND, DRHAGIS, all disjoint from our experimental datasets. 6.R1-W6: PraNet, weights, and coefficients. PraNet’s reverse attention refines weak boundaries, matching our OD-preservation goal. The spatial coefficients (1+10σ for vessels, 1+5σ for OD; Eq. 7) are task-aware: higher for sparse vessels, lower for the compact OD. Global weights λ_v=0.01, λ_od=0.04 (Eq. 8) were tuned on the validation set. 7.R2-W1, R3-W2: Downstream protocol. Downstream models — classification: ConvNeXt-Tiny; segmentation: U-Net++ (vessels), PraNet (OD). All trained with AdamW (lr=1e-4, cosine annealing, 100 epochs) using each model’s official loss. Segmentation models reuse ACR teachers’ architectures but train on disjoint data (R1-W5). Identical protocol across methods: each downstream model is trained once on HQ and frozen; enhanced outputs from all methods are tested on the same frozen model—no retraining. 8.R2-W2: Baseline selection. Our baselines cover both SOTA fundus enhancement methods (MDA, OTE, GFE) and methods from related fields whose algorithms are suitable for fundus enhancement; methods relying on modality-specific mechanisms (e.g., algorithms targeting CT/MRI-specific noise) are excluded. Against SOTA fundus methods alone, WaveDE still leads by 4.66–9.24 dB PSNR (Tab. 1). 9.R2-W3: Direct analysis of LF/HF experts. We agree this would help. As indirect evidence, Tab. 1 (w/o FD) shows Local artifact and Blur benefit most, and Fig. 2 shows our model attains the smallest LF and HF residuals. An LF/HF discussion will be added in the camera-ready. We will explore w/o LF and w/o HF ablations in future work. 10.R3-W4: Failure cases. We acknowledge this omission. From Tab. 1, the most apparent relative weakness is the colour subset, where WaveDE’s PSNR (33.73 dB) trails other subsets (39+ dB). This failure mode will be discussed in camera-ready.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper tackles an important problem and presents a technically solid solution with strong empirical results. The reviewers are generally positive, but several issues need to be clarified before the work can be fully assessed. The main concern is limited validation on real-world degradations. The model is trained on synthetic corruptions, while real clinical degradations are more complex. Current evaluation relies largely on synthetic settings, with only limited real-data validation. The authors should better justify the clinical applicability and, if possible, provide additional analysis on real degraded images. Second, experimental protocol and fairness need clarification. There is potential overlap between training and downstream datasets, and it is unclear whether splits are strictly disjoint. The downstream evaluation setup (e.g., retraining vs. direct inference) is also not clearly described. Baseline selection could be more focused on relevant fundus enhancement methods. Third, methodological analysis is incomplete. Key components (e.g., structural guidance, frequency decoupling, VMamba choice) are not sufficiently isolated or justified through ablations. More insight into what each module contributes would strengthen the claims. Finally, efficiency and reproducibility are underreported, including model size, runtime, and training details. Addressing these points would significantly strengthen the paper. | After considering the reviews and the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important problem in fundus image enhancement and presents a coherent framework supported by strong empirical results across restoration, downstream analysis, and out-of-distribution evaluation. The rebuttal adequately addresses most of the major concerns regarding experimental protocols, reproducibility, and evaluation fairness. While concerns remain regarding the reliance on synthetic degradations and the need for broader real-world validation, these limitations do not undermine the main findings of the paper. Overall, I believe the contribution is technically sound, practically relevant, and sufficiently supported by the presented evidence. Recommendation: Accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers generally viewed the problem as important and the design as coherent, and two reviewers supported acceptance after the rebuttal. I also recommend acceptance, while noting that the paper should be framed carefully around its synthetic-degradation setting. WaveDE addresses a practical problem in fundus image enhancement, where compound degradations can harm both visual quality and downstream analysis. The proposed wavelet-routed dual-expert design is well matched to this setting: low-frequency correction, high-frequency restoration, high-frequency injection in the VAE decoder, and anatomical consistency regularization form a coherent framework. The empirical results are strong, including PSNR/SSIM, ablations, downstream classification/segmentation, and OOD evaluation. The rebuttal also clarifies several important points about data splits, downstream protocols, teacher datasets, and deployment cost. The main limitation is that training and much of the evaluation rely on synthetic degradations, so claims about real clinical robustness should be stated with caution. For the camera-ready version, the authors should incorporate the rebuttal clarifications on split disjointness, downstream evaluation protocol, teacher-network training data, inference cost, and baseline selection. They should also clearly discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, the limited real-degradation validation, and the remaining failure mode on color-related degradations. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the rebuttal and other reviewers’ comments, I think the authors have reasonably addressed the main concerns.

title: Weakly-Supervised Temporal Decomposition with Graph Neural Networks for Parkinsonian Turning Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strength of this paper is the proposed architecture, which introduces a novel and well-motivated approach to Parkinsonian turning assessment. The ablation study is clearly demonstrates the contribution of each component. The comparison with existing methods is also convincing, with the proposed method outperforming all baselines across all reported metrics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Several comments on the text: 1) The terms task-specific and phase-specific temporal structure are central to the paper but never explicitly defined. Adding a short definition in the Introduction would help readers coming from a general ML background. 2) The term ‘phase boundaries’ is used in the Introduction before being formally defined in Section 3.2.I would suggest either adding a brief informal definition at first use in the Introduction, or at minimum a forward reference to Section 3.2. 3) In the Introduction, two consecutive sentences essentially say the same thing: ‘learning phase boundaries directly from video-level diagnostic labels alone’ and ‘without any frame-level supervision’ convey the same idea. I’d suggest merging these into one sentence to avoid repetition. 4) The claim that frame-level annotations are impractical in clinical settings is made in Related Work and then repeated again in Section 3.2. 5) The limitation of fixed skeleton topology (treating all joint connections equally) is only introduced in Section 3.3, but I think it would fit better in the Introduction alongside the global pooling limitation. This way readers understand from the beginning that the paper addresses both temporal and spatial rigidity in existing methods, which better reflects the full scope of the contribution. More broadly, some motivational points are repeated across sections in slightly different wording. A careful pass to either consolidate or use forward/backward references would tighten the paper considerably. 6) What is the difference between the ST-GCN baseline in Table 1 (which achieves 61.71% AUC) and the ST-GCN method in Table 3 (69.94% AUC)? Should they be identical?

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper tackles a clinically relevant and well-motivated problem. Turning is a meaningful indicator in PD assessment, and skeleton-based analysis provides a practical and privacy-preserving representation. The methodological contribution is clear and reasonably novel. The approach goes beyond standard temporal attention by explicitly discovering ordered temporal instances in a weakly-supervised manner and integrating them with GCN-based modeling. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback. We address the major concerns below. [Q1] Presentation suggestions (R1-W1–W5) All five presentation suggestions will be addressed in the revision. [Q2] Baseline vs full model of ST-GCN: Table 1 and Table 3 (R1-W6) The “ST-GCN baseline” in Table 1 is our lightweight 2-block encoder, serving as the minimal ablation baseline (61.71% AUC). The “ST-GCN [27]” in Table 3 is the full Yan et al. architecture, trained under the same protocol (69.94% AUC). The 8.23% gap reflects this capacity difference, not an inconsistency; a clarifying footnote will be added. [Q3] Training constraints and link between losses and motion saliency (R2-W1,W2) The decomposition branch is architecturally decoupled, but its boundary estimates remain explicitly constrained. Boundary scores s(t) are computed from [f(t);Δf(t)], capturing motor state and motion change, and are constrained by a learnable position prior, temporally ordered K=3 masks, and L_sparse/L_smooth. The auxiliary losses suppress dense or fragmented detections. By design, non-differentiable boundary selection prevents L_cls from directly biasing boundary locations, preserving label independent transition discovery, while the resulting masks still serve as weights in mask-weighted pooling and ultimately determine the sequence representation used for classification. We will clarify this path and describe the learned regions as soft temporal transition candidates, not ground truth phases. The +5.93% AUC gain over fixed decomposition (Table 1, (p<0.01)) supports this design. [Q4] Adaptive adjacency design (R2-W3) Physical skeleton topology serves as an anatomically informed architectural prior, constraining learnable adjacency to anatomically valid connections, limiting parameter space on clinical-scale data and preserving interpretability of learned edge weights. We agree that non-local dynamics carry clinical value; capturing such interactions is a natural direction for future work. [Q5] Statistical robustness (R2-W4) All tables report mean±standard deviation across the same subject-level 5-fold CV. Table 1 already includes paired t-tests ( *p<0.01, ** p<0.001), confirming each component is statistically significant; the last row of Tables 2–3 is also statistically significant over all other configurations; significance notes will be added in the revision. [Q6] Clinical characterization (R2) Our evaluation uses the REMAP dataset. PD diagnosis followed the UK Brain Bank Criteria. The 1,294 sequences (773 PD, 521 HC) derive from 12 PD and 12 HC participants. H&Y=2.3±0.8 (entry criterion ≤3, mild-to-moderate PD); per-H&Y-stage breakdown is not reported. MDS-UPDRS III=36.8±23.0.A clinical summary will be added to Section 4.1.Subject-level 5-fold CV prevents data leakage; fold assignment was not stratified by severity score, as our framework operates solely on video-level diagnostic label; severity-stratified analysis remains future work. [Q7] Interpretability claims (R3-W1) We agree that the learned segments should not be interpreted as validated biomechanical phases. “Early/Mid/Late-Turn” are temporal-ordering names for soft instances, not frame-level phase annotations. Fig. 2 provides qualitative interpretation only: PD shows higher late-instance attention than HC (α₃=0.51 vs 0.36), and the anatomical map emphasizes lower-limb connections, consistent with prior PD turning/gait findings. We will replace “clinically meaningful phase boundaries” with “soft temporal transition candidates/instances” and state that direct frame-level phase validation remains future work. [Q8] Reproducibility: missing hyperparameters (R3-W2) Missing λ_s=0.05 and λ_m=0.1 will be added to Section 4.1; others are already reported. Code will be released upon acceptance. [Q9] Single-dataset (R3-W3) We acknowledge this limitation. REMAP is among the few public labeled datasets for PD turning assessment, and cross-cohort generalization remains future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There are some discrepancies among the three reviewers, consisting of one weak reject, one weak accept, and one accept. The main contributions of the paper include the proposed dual-branch weakly supervised temporal decomposition framework, that is evaluated on a clinical dataset with promising results. Meanwhile, there are a number of aspects of the work that raise concerns. It would be beneficial if the authors provide further input and clarifications in the areas specifically brought out by the reviewers, including but not limited to, how to ensure constrained training process in current system esp. by engaging the current loss functions, empirical studies of the statistical robustness aspect; details of the empirical evaluations; possibly overstated claims; reproducibility; improvement of the current presentation. | Most of the major concerns have been addressed by the rebuttal. That said, there remain concerns such as the limited number of subjects in dataset. The authors are encouraged to carefully follow the reviews and revise the draft accordingly, if it is eventually accepted by this MICCAI. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper deals with the automated analysis of the Parkinson’s disease turning assessment, which is a clinically well-motivated problem. Specifically, the authors have proposed a dual-branch architecture based on skeleton-based processing backbones. The reviewers identified that this is an important and clinically motivated problem to be solved and appreciate the dual-branch architecture. However, several concerns were raised regarding the choice of the loss functions and how they relate to the main goal of the paper and most importantly the limited size of the dataset especially in terms of the number of subjects (only limited to 12PD and 12 healthy controls), which questions the generalzability and robustness and experimental validation of the claims of the proposed framework. Moreover, I also think that several major baselines in the general skeleton-based human activity understanding domain are missing - for instance HyperGCN (modeling skeleton sequences as a hypergraph). The authors built on the very old baselines of skeleton-based GCN processing where ST-GCN was one of the first baselines, but have not explored how more recent approaches compare to it. Thus, the gains presented by the authors may be due to the inherent incapability of methods like ST-GCN to extract relevant features necessary for this task. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, two reviewers are satisfied with the rebuttal. The authors have properly addressed most major concerns including interpretability, reproducibility and architectural discrepancy. Yet limited participant count and absence of severity-stratified analysis weaken clinical generalization. Overall, this is a good paper and the recommendation is Accept.
